en: *The Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs Through the Successive Dynasties*,
Volume One, compiled by Nianchang of Huating while serving as the Abbot of Dazhongxiangfu Chan Monastery in Jiaxing Prefecture.

*The Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs Through the Ages*, Volume One: The Verses of the Seven Buddhas. The verse of the ninth hundred and ninety-eighth Buddha of the past *Vibhāṣī* (Vipaśyin) Buddha in the *Prabhava-kalpa* (Aeon of Radiance) states:
The body is born from within the signless,
just like various forms produced by illusion;
the mind-consciousness of the illusory person is fundamentally non-existent.
Both sin and merit are empty and have no abiding place.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
"When the human lifespan was eighty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world."
He was of the Kṣatriya caste,
of the Kauṇḍinya clan;
his father was Bandhu and his mother was Bandhumatī.
He resided in the city of Bandhumatī and sat beneath a śirīṣa tree to preach the Dharma.
In three assemblies, he delivered thirty-four thousand eight hundred people across the threshold of liberation.
There were two who possessed the divine feet:
the first was named Khandaka,
and the second was named Tiṣya.
The attendant was Aśoka.
His successor was Fangying.
Śikhin Buddha, the nine hundred and ninety-ninth Tathāgata of the Bhadrakalpa, spoke in verse:
The arising of all wholesome dharmas is fundamentally an illusion;
the commission of all unwholesome karmas is likewise an illusion.
The body is like a mass of foam; the mind is like the wind.
It is manifested as an illusion, devoid of root and lacking intrinsic nature.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
"When the human lifespan is seventy thousand years, this Buddha appears in the world."
He was of the Kṣatriya caste,
of the Kauṇḍinya clan,
and his father was named Vimala.
The Mother, Radiant Splendor,
dwelt in the city of Radiant Appearance;
sitting beneath a Puṇḍarīka tree, she preached the Dharma.
In three assemblies, he delivered two hundred and fifty thousand people.
He had two disciples with supernormal powers (ṛddhi):
the first was named Abhibhū.
The second was named Babha;
his attendant was Kṣemacārin;
his son was Aparimita.
The verse for the first of the thousand Buddhas of the Auspicious Kalpa (Bhadrakalpa), Viśvabhū Buddha, says:
"The body is provisionally constructed from the four great elements;
the mind is fundamentally without birth, arising only due to objects."
If the external object does not exist, the mind likewise does not exist;
sin and merit arise like illusions and likewise perish.
As the *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
When the human lifespan was sixty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world.
He was of the Kṣatriya caste and belonged to the Kauṇḍinya clan.
His father was named Good Lamp;
his mother was named Renowned Virtue;
they resided in the city of Beyond Analogy.
He sat beneath a *bhallāṭa* tree and preached the Dharma.
In two assemblies, he delivered thirteen hundred thousand people.
His supernormal powers were of two kinds.
The first is named Bhramara;
the second is named Uttama.
His attendant is named Śānti.
Son, you are of wondrous enlightenment.
Kāśyapa Buddha, who is currently the first honored one of the Bhadrakalpa, spoke in verse:
"To see that the body has no reality is the Buddha-body."
To realize that the mind is like an illusion is the Buddha’s illusion;
to realize that the fundamental nature of body and mind is empty—
how does such a person differ from the Buddha?
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
"When the human lifespan was forty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world;
he was born into a brahmin family."
His clan was Kāśyapa;
his father was Riddha,
and his mother was Suprabhā.
He resided in the city of Ānandapura and sat beneath a śirīṣa tree to preach the Dharma;
in a single assembly, he delivered forty thousand people across [to liberation].
There are two divine feet (ṛddhipāda): first, Sani; second, Vīlu.
The attendant was Sujāta;
his son was Jinaśreṣṭha.
The verse concerning Krakucchanda Buddha, the second honored one of the Bhadrakalpa, says:
The Buddha does not see the Buddha, yet he knows this is the Buddha.
If there were truly a knowing that was distinct from the Buddha, it would not be the Buddha.
The wise are able to know that the nature of offenses is empty.
He was composed and fearless regarding birth and death.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states that this Buddha appeared in the world when the human lifespan was thirty thousand years.
He was of the Brahmin caste,
of the Kāśyapa clan,
and his father was Mahāgopa.
The Mother, Bhadraśrī,
dwelt in the city of Viśuddha;
she sat beneath an udumbara tree and preached the Dharma.
In one assembly, he delivered thirty thousand people.
His second [disciple] with supernormal powers was Śūrpaka.
Second was Udraka;
his attendant was Ananda,
and his son was Śāstṛ.
The verse of Kāśyapa Buddha, the third honored one of the Bhadrakalpa, says:
"The nature of all sentient beings is pure;
from the beginning, they are unborn and there is nothing to be extinguished."
This very body and mind are born of illusion;
within these illusory transformations, there is neither sin nor merit.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
When the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world.
He was born into a Brahmin family and belonged to the Kāśyapa clan.
His father was Brahmadatta and his mother was Dhanavatī;
they resided in the city of Vārāṇasī.
Sitting beneath a nyagrodha tree, he preached the Dharma;
in a single assembly, he delivered twenty thousand people across [to liberation].
His second [great] supernatural power.
First, Tiṣya;
second, Bharadvāja;
and the attendant was Kalyāṇamitra.
The Son advanced his army.
Śākyamuni Buddha, the fourth honored one of the Bhadrakalpa, spoke in verse:
"The Dharma is fundamentally without dharma."
Non-dharmas are themselves dharmas;
now, at the time of entrusting non-dharmas,
how have dharmas ever been dharmas?
He was of the Kṣatriya caste;
his father was Śuddhodana,
and his mother was Mahāmāyā.
He resided in the city of Śrāvastī and sat beneath the Bodhi tree to preach the Dharma;
in one assembly, there were one thousand two hundred and fifty disciples.
He delivered countless people.
His two disciples endowed with supernormal powers were first Śāriputra and second Maudgalyāyana.
Ānanda was his attendant,
and Rāhula was his son;
thus the ancient Buddhas have appeared in the world in an endless succession.
It cannot be fully known or enumerated.
The World-Honored One has said:
"By means of the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision..."
He contemplates that which is remote as if it were today;
thus, according to the *Buddhanāmasūtra*,
he records the thousand Tathāgatas of the past and present kalpas.
Coming down to Śākyamuni, only the seven Buddhas are designated.
The *Āgama Sūtra* states:
"The power of diligence of the seven Buddhas."
Emitting light that extinguishes the darkness,
they each sat beneath various trees and therein attained perfect enlightenment.
The translation of the Buddhas and Patriarchs’ Verses was produced by the eminent monk Yunkai, together with the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas from India,
at the kingdom of Kucha.
The preface and main text were recorded in the sixth year of the Datong era of the Liang dynasty.

*The Treatise on Manifesting What is Known* (Tshad ma rnam par nges pa’i bstan bcos tshig le’ur byas pa rigs pa’i rgyan), spoken by the Imperial Preceptor Phag mo gru pa Byams pa dpal, was translated by Śālarapa, the Great Master of Buddhist Wisdom and Tripitaka-holder Dharmatā, who was appointed as the General Superintendent of the Buddhist Teachings for Jianghuai, Fujian, and other regions.
2. Chapter on the Receptacle World. The essential substance of the receptacle world is composed of the four great elements arising in various ways;
therefore, earth is solid, water is moist, fire is warm, and wind is mobile.
The most extremely subtle among these primary elements (mahābhūta) is called the atom (paramāṇu),
also known as the infinitesimal particle (aṇu);
it cannot be further analyzed or divided.
Seven of those atoms constitute one subtle atom (*paramāṇu*);
seven of those subtle atoms constitute one mote of dust (*rajas*);
and seven of those motes of dust constitute one particle that penetrates gold (*tapanīya-rajas*).
Seven *paramāṇu-rajas* (gold-dust atoms) constitute one *trasareṇu-rajas* (water-dust atom).
Seven *trasareṇu-rajas* constitute one *śaśa-roma-rajas* (hare-hair dust atom).
Seven *śaśa-roma-rajas* constitute one *avi-roma-rajas* (sheep-hair dust atom).
Seven particles of sheep’s wool constitute one particle of cow’s hair;
seven particles of cow’s hair constitute one particle of dust motes in a sunbeam;
and seven particles of dust motes in a sunbeam constitute the measure of one nit.
Seven *likṣā* make one *yūka*;
seven *yūka* make one barley grain (*yava*);
and seven barley grains make one finger-joint (*aṅguli-parvan*).
Three finger-joints constitute one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
Twenty-four finger-breadths laid side-by-side constitute one cubit (*hasta*). Four cubits constitute one bow (*dhanus*).
Five hundred bows measure one *krośa*.
Eight *krośas* make one *yojana*.
This is the measurement of the physical dimensions of the world,
which constitutes the causal basis for the formation of the world.
It is produced by the collective karma of all sentient beings.
How is it formed?
From within the realm of space, winds arise from the ten directions and strike against one another.
Solid, dense, and immovable, it constitutes a wondrous wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*).
Its color is bluish-white, it is exceedingly vast and solid,
and its depth is sixteen *lakṣa* yojanas.
Its vast extent is incalculable.
From heat, clouds called "Golden Treasury" arise,
which pour down great rain that rests upon the wind.
It is called the Bottom of the Ocean;
it is eleven lakṣas and twenty thousand yojanas deep,
and twelve lakṣas and three thousand four hundred and fifty yojanas wide.
As that water strikes and surges upward, it solidifies into gold,
just as when boiled milk cools and a film forms on the surface;
this is the Golden Wheel of the Earth.
Therefore, when the water wheel diminishes until it is only eight lakṣas thick,
the remainder transforms into gold,
with a thickness of three lakṣas and twenty thousand yojanas.
The extent of the Golden Wheel is equal to that of the Water Wheel;
its circumference is three times this,
totaling thirty-six lakṣas, ten thousand, three hundred and fifty yojanas.
Below that wind-circle at the base of the Sahā world-system,
and beneath the four continents which rest upon the two circles of earth and water,
a great rain falls upon the earth-circle, thereby forming the great ocean.
The superior-grade accumulations, struck by the wind, form Mount Sumeru;
the medium-grade accumulations form the seven golden mountains;
and the inferior-grade accumulations form the Cakravāḍa Mountains.
The miscellaneous items are gathered together as the four continents and so forth.
As for the substance of Mount Sumeru,
its eastern side is composed of silver, the southern of lapis lazuli, the western of crystal, and the northern of gold.
The other seven [mountains] consist solely of gold.
The lands of the four continents and so forth are composed of various substances.
That Cakravāḍa mountain, however, consists solely of iron.
Its height extends eighty thousand yojanas into the water;
compared to all other mountains, it is preeminent and sublime,
and is therefore called "Wondrously High" (Sumeru).
Thereafter, as for the seventh of the golden mountains,
it is Yugandhara,
which is forty thousand yojanas in height.
Second is Īṣādhāra,
twenty thousand yojanas high;
third is Khadiraka.
It is ten thousand yojanas high;
its four terraces of śāla trees are five thousand yojanas high.
The fifth is Aśvakarṇa,
two thousand five hundred yojanas high;
the sixth is Vinataka.
It is twelve hundred and fifty *yojana*s high.
There are seven Nimindhara mountains, each six hundred and twenty-five *yojana*s high. The *Zanglun shu* (Commentary on the Abhidharmakośa) states:
1. Yugandhara Mountain;
2. Īṣādhara Mountain;
3. Kailāśa (or Khadiraka) Mountain.
Fourth is Mount Sudarśana;
fifth is Mount Aśvakarṇa;
sixth is Mount Gajodara.
Beyond the seven Fish-Mouth Mountains and the four great continents lies the Cakravāḍa mountain range.
It is two hundred and twelve and a half yojanas high;
their respective widths are each equal to the height of the water they emerge from.
The places where the various nāga kings sport among the seven golden mountains are called the Playful Seas (*krīḍā-samudra*).
Among the seven seas situated between the eight mountains,
the one closest to Mount Sumeru is the Yugaṃdhara Sea.
It is eighty thousand yojanas wide.
The second, the Īṣādhāra Sea,
is forty thousand yojanas wide.
Third is the Khadira-ko Sea,
twenty thousand yojanas in width;
fourth is the Tāṃsala Sea.
It is ten thousand yojanas wide.
The five Aśvakarṇa seas are five thousand yojanas wide.
The sixth is the Vinītaka Sea,
two thousand five hundred yojanas in breadth.
The seventh is the Nimindhara Sea.
It is one thousand two hundred and fifty yojanas in breadth and is filled with water possessing the eight virtues;
its eight mountains and seven seas are all square in shape.
The outer ocean is salty in taste.
From Mount Nimindhara to Mount Cakravāḍa,
the distance between these two mountains is three hundred and twenty-two thousand yojanas.
Although the waters of the outer ocean have no distinct divisions,
they appear white in the eastern sea due to the color of Mount Sumeru.
The Southern Ocean is blue in color;
the Western Ocean is red in color;
the Northern Ocean is yellow in color.
Because these various forms appear therein,
it is called the "Four Seas.
Its circumference is thirty-six lakṣas and seven hundred and fifty yojanas.
The outer Cakravāḍa Mountains have a circumference of thirty-six lakṣas, two thousand six hundred and twenty-five yojanas.
Beyond them lies the southern continent of Jambudvīpa in the southern ocean.
It is shaped like a carriage box;
it is three and a half yojanas wide toward the Cakravāḍa mountains,
while the other three sides are wider.
Each is two thousand yojanas [in length],
with a circumference of six thousand three and a half yojanas.
There are two intermediate islands.
To the east is Camara, here translated as "Cat-ox"; to the west is Varacāmara, here translated as "Superior Cat-ox.
In the center of Jambudvīpa is the kingdom of Magadha, the place where the Buddhas of the three periods of time are born.
Next, to the north of this, crossing nine Black Mountains,
there is a Great Snowy Mountain named Śrīmat.
On the northern side of that mountain is the Fragrant Intoxication Mountain (Gandhamādana).
Between these two mountains dwells a great nāga king named Anavatapta;
the lake where he resides is called Anavatapta (translated here as "Unheated"), which is square in shape, measuring fifty yojanas on each side.
It extends for two hundred yojanas in circumference.
The pond is filled throughout with water possessing the eight meritorious qualities.
From within this pond, four great rivers flow forth.
To the east is the Ganges River;
from the mouth of the elephant flows silver sand, which,
together with five hundred tributary rivers, flows into the eastern sea.
To the south of Xindu,
the river flows out from the mouth of an ox;
its lapis lazuli sands flow together with five hundred tributary rivers back toward the South Sea.
The River Vālukā flows from the horse’s mouth with sands of crystal;
together with five hundred tributary rivers, it flows into the western ocean.
To the north is the Sitā River;
golden sand flows from the mouth of the Lion,
and together with five hundred rivers, it returns to the Northern Sea.
These four rivers flow from Lake Anavatapta, circling it seven times to the right before proceeding in their respective directions.
Twenty yojanas to the north of Mount Gandhamādana,
there is a cliff named Nanda.
Each rock face is fifty yojanas in extent;
it is two hundred yojanas in circumference and three and a half yojanas in height.
Furthermore, there are eight thousand small crags.
On the northern side of these crags, twenty yojanas away,
stands the king of śāla trees named Supratiṣṭhita.
Its roots entered the earth to a depth of forty bows,
and it rose eighty bows in height;
seven rows of trees were arranged in succession, surrounding it on all sides.
Twenty yojanas to the east lies the Mandākinī Pond;
it is circular in shape and fifty yojanas in width.
Its circumference is one hundred and fifty yojanas.
Furthermore, there are eight thousand small ponds filled with water possessing the eight virtues.
Within it is a lotus flower;
its petals are like ox-hide,
and its stalk is like a chariot axle.
The flowers are like chariot wheels and their flavor is as sweet as honey.
In this place there is also the elephant king named Supratiṣṭhita, which Śakra mounts when he goes forth to battle.
Accompanied by eight thousand elephants, he dwelt at Mount Kanaka during the four months of winter;
he dwelt at the Abhyavakāśa during the four months of summer;
and he dwelt at the Mandākinī pool during the four months of the rainy season.
Beside the Lake Anavatapta stands a Jambū tree;
its fruits are delicious in flavor and as large as jars.
When they ripen and fall into the water, they produce the sound "jambū."
A dragon transformed into a fish devoured these fruits;
the remnants, encountering a current, became Jambūnada gold.
Because of the name of this tree, it is called Jambudvīpa.
To the west of this continent lies the country of Oḍḍiyāna,
where the Great Vajra Palace, the abode of the Vidyādharas, is situated;
from there, the Vajrayāna teachings were transmitted.
In the Southern Sea there is a mountain called Dhānakaṭaka;
the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara dwells upon its summit,
and the Noble Mother Tārā dwells at its base.
To the east are five peaks where Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva resides;
there are sixteen great kingdoms and thousands of small kingdoms.
Furthermore, there are three hundred and sixty thousand kinds of people and seven hundred and twenty varieties of distinct languages.
To the east of the outer ocean lies the continent called Videha.
Its shape is like a half-moon;
it measures three hundred and fifty yojanas along the side facing Mount Sumeru,
and sixty yojanas along the other side.
Its circumference is six thousand three hundred and fifty yojanas.
On its two sides are two intermediate continents:

Uttarakuru (translated here as "Body") to the north, and Aparagoyānī (translated here as "Superior Body") to the south. These three continents exceed the other continents by the height of seven tala trees.
Some say that because the people of this continent possess upright and dignified features and their bodies are superior,
it is called "Superior Body" (Videha).
Beyond that outer sea lies the northern continent, called Kuru.
Its shape is four-cornered,
resembling a square.
Each side is two thousand yojanas,
with a circumference of eight thousand yojanas;
on two sides of that continent, there are two intermediate continents.

First is named Kuru, which means "Possessing Excellence"; second is Uttarakuru, which means "Possessing Excellence on the Border. All the enjoyments of the people of those continents arise from wish-fulfilling trees.
Seven days before his passing,
the wish-fulfilling tree emitted an unpleasant sound,
which it explained, saying:
They die after seven days.
Some say that because the inhabitants of this continent have short tongues, they are immediately cut off and eaten by flesh-eating demons (*piśāca*);
thus it is called Kaurava.
This is the region of Unpleasant Sound.
To the west of the outer ocean lies the continent called Go-dānīya,
which is shaped like a full moon.
It is two thousand five hundred yojanas in diameter and seven thousand five hundred yojanas in circumference.
It contains two intermediate continents.

To the south is Śāṭhā, which means "Possessing Deceit"; to the north is Uttaramantriṇa, which means "Superior in Ritual. Because the people of that continent mostly possess many precious cattle and engage in trade, it is called Go-dānīya (Cattle-Trade).
The continents, oceans, mountains, and so forth, extend eighty thousand *yojanas* downward;
because they are close to the Golden Ground (*kāñcanamayī bhūmi*), they are near Jambudvīpa.
As for the Nakṣatra-dvīpa, Kaṇṭaka-dvīpa, Suvarṇa-dvīpa, Candra-dvīpa, and others:
This refers to Jambudvīpa;
it is the same for the other great continents and the minor islands as well.
Forty thousand yojanas above this,
there is a supreme, solid wind-circle that is utterly pure and unobstructed.
It revolves from right to left.
The sun, moon, stars, and the gods who dwell in the sky reside there in dependence upon it.
3. As for the solar disk:
It is composed of fire-pearls;
its diameter is fifty-one yojanas,
and its circumference is one hundred and fifty-three yojanas.
It is six yojanas thick, plus eighteen sixtieths of a yojana;
it has a golden rim above, and upon that,
there are further layers of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and white coral.
It forms four corners.
The palaces where the Sun Deity and others reside move by means of the wind;
in one day and night, they circumambulate the four great continents.
When the sun moves toward the north, the days are long;
when it moves toward the south, they are short;
and when it moves between the two directions, day and night are equal.
Due to the light of their place of movement, there are cold and heat,
serving as the boundaries between winter and summer;
they travel north for six months and south for six months.
When they have traveled halfway, he said:
"The sun and moon revolve, and the wheel of the stars completes its circuit; this is called one year."
4. As for the lunar disc, it is composed of water-crystal;
its diameter is fifty yojanas.
It is one hundred and fifty yojanas in circumference and six yojanas and eighteen parts in thickness; upon it,
there are further [deposits of] gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and white jade.
The palaces where the Moon Deity and others reside are four-cornered.
It is due to the varying distances between those suns and moons that their shadows increase or decrease.
By increasing by one part, the first half of the fifteen parts is completed;
this is called "full.
By decreasing by one part, the second half arises, and its own reflection covers those fifteen parts until they are finished.
It is said that they are not complete.
Because of their increase and decrease, they are called "empty of the past" (宿空);
because of the single day and night, they are called "ground of the past" (宿地).
These thirty days are called one month.
As for the various lunar mansions (nakṣatras),
they are celestial palaces dwelling in space, composed of various jewels.
Their shapes are all circular;
the small ones are one *go-vyūha* in size,
and the medium ones are three *go-vyūhas*.
The Great Six Ox-Howls are three times its circumference and are governed by the hosts of the Four Kings.
6. As for Mount Sumeru, it has four terraces.
From the water’s edge upward, they extend ten thousand yojanas apart.
That is the first terrace;
it extends sixteen thousand yojanas out from the side of Mount Sumeru and rises ten thousand yojanas upward.
It consists of two tiers;
they extend outwards for eight thousand yojanas and rise upwards at intervals of ten thousand yojanas.
That is, it has three tiers;
they extend outwards for four thousand yojanas,
and are separated from one another by ten thousand yojanas as they ascend.
That Mount Sumeru has four terraces,
each extending two thousand yojanas outward.
At its summit are four corners,
each featuring a prominent peak four and a half yojanas high.
It is one hundred and twenty-five yojanas wide and five hundred yojanas in circumference;
a yakṣa deity dwells therein.
On the summit of this mountain is the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
In its center is the city called Sudarśana,
which is composed entirely of pure gold.
It is one and a half yojanas in height;
each side is two thousand five hundred yojanas,
making its circumference ten thousand yojanas.
The body of that city is made of gold and is adorned with one hundred and one varieties of miscellaneous jewels;
its ground is as soft as tūla-cotton.
On the four sides of this city, there are sixteen thousand jeweled pillars, jeweled beams, jeweled rafters, and jeweled eaves.
On each of the four sides, there are four gates, and furthermore, there are thousands of small side-gates.
At the four great crossroads there were various smaller lanes;
by the side of each of the four gates,
five hundred devaputras, all clad in sturdy armor, guarded those gates.
Within the city is the palace of Śakra called the Most Excellent Place (Vaijayanta),
also known as the Palace of Extraordinary Excellence;
it is square in shape.
It is four hundred and fifty yojanas in height;
each side is two hundred and fifty yojanas;
its circumference is one thousand yojanas.
There are one hundred and one defensive towers;
each defensive tower has seven multi-storied pavilions,
and each precious pavilion has seven small pavilions.
Each small pavilion has seven ponds;
each pond has seven lotuses;
upon each lotus there are seven boys and seven girls.
Various kinds of music were performed,
and they enjoyed themselves with song and dance.
To the east of the city of Sudarśana, there were various means of transport.
It is called the Garden of Chariots (Cakravāḍa),
which is one thousand yojanas high.
To the south, bordering the battlefield, is the Garden of Coarseness (Rudra-vana).
The western area for practicing various activities is called the Grove of Mixed Fragrances;
the northern area for recreation is named the Grove of Joy.
Their length and breadth are the same as those previously described.
Outside these gardens and others, at a distance of twenty yojanas, there are excellent lands called Saṃtāna (Multitude of Chariots),
Pāruṣyaka (Coarse and Harsh), Miśraka (Mixed), and Nandana (Joyful);
their dimensions are equal to those of the four gardens.
To the northeast of Sudarśana is the wish-fulfilling tree,
named Pārijāta, also called the Maṇḍalaja tree.
Its roots extend fifty yojanas deep;
it rises a hundred yojanas high;
and its branches spread fifty yojanas in every direction.
It can bestow sensual pleasures.
Below is a flat rock called Arimoli-ge.
Its color is white like fine cotton cloth; each face is fifty yojanas [in width], and its circumference is two hundred yojanas.
It is the place where the gods assemble to the southwest of Sudarśana.
It is named the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā).
It is nine hundred yojanas in circumference and is circular in shape.
In the center of this hall is the throne of Śakra,
made entirely of pure gold.
Surrounding that throne are thirty-two thrones for his attendant ministers.
They are all arrayed together.
Above the Heaven of the Thirty-three,
at a distance of eighty thousand yojanas, [lies the next realm].
Within the realm of space, resting upon the wind,
there is the celestial palace of the Vaiśravaṇa-devas (the Devas Free from Strife), composed of various jewels;
its dimensions are twice those of the summit of Mount Sumeru.
It is situated one hundred and sixty million yojanas above,
resting upon the wind within the realm of space.
Composed of various jewels, the Tuṣita celestial palace is equal in size to the Saṃtuṣita [palace].
It is twice as long and wide;
its upper limit reaches three hundred and twenty thousand yojanas,
and it rests upon the wind within the realm of space.
The celestial palaces of the Nirmāṇarati gods, composed of various jewels,
are twice as large in length and breadth as those of Tuṣita;
they are situated at a height of six hundred and forty thousand yojanas above.
Within the realm of space, it rests supported by wind.
Composed of various jewels, the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods is equal in size to that of the Nirmāṇarati heaven,
with its length and breadth being twice as great.
This is the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Above it is the first dhyāna (*prathamadhyāna*).
Thus, the four continents, the seven mountain ranges, Mount Sumeru, the Cakravāḍa mountains, the six heavens of the desire realm, and the first dhyāna, and so forth, [constitute this world].
That is to say, one thousand four-continent world-systems constitute a small chiliocosm,
which is surrounded by a single Iron Ring Mountain (Cakravāḍa).
One thousand such small chiliocosms constitute a medium chiliocosm.
Each of these is surrounded by a single Iron Ring Mountain (*Cakravāḍa*).
When one thousand of these intermediate thousandfold worlds reach their full number of thousands, they constitute a Great Trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*),
which is surrounded by a single Great Iron Ring Mountain.
In this manner, there are ten billion such world-systems of four continents, all distributed throughout space.
In the dark regions between the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*) and the various continents and mountains, there is neither day nor night, and one cannot see even a hand raised.

The extent of the First Dhyāna Heaven is equal to that of the world-system of four continents; the extent of the Second Dhyāna Heaven is equal to that of a small chiliocosm; and the extent of the Third Dhyāna Heaven is equal to that of a medium chiliocosm.
The dimensions of the fourth dhyāna heaven are equal to those of the trichiliocosm, and their distances from one another all increase twofold at each successive level;
this is called the realm of form (rūpadhātu). As for the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu):
There is no separate location.
If there were one who is born [there], from where would they pass away?
They are born in that very place while abiding in the formless meditative absorption (ārūpya-samādhi).
Therefore, it is called "formless.
Seven: The Chapter on the World of Sentient Beings states that the world of sentient beings generally comprises six types.
The first is the hells.
Second, hungry ghosts;
third, animals;
fourth, humans.
Fifth, non-gods; sixth, gods.
What are the meanings of these six categories?
It is called "hell" (niraya) because one's limbs are hacked and destroyed;
it is a place where one is tormented by hunger and thirst.
Therefore they are called hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Because they move by crawling sideways,
they are called animals (*tiryagyoni*).
Because the mind engages in much conceptual discrimination,
it is called "man" (pudgala).
This is the meaning of *maṇuṣya*.
Although their bodies and enjoyments are similar to those of the gods,
they are slightly inferior;
this may be due to the absence of wine.
Therefore it is said that they are not devas.
The meaning of asura is:
born from the Brahmakāyika heaven, they engage in play and amusement.
Alternatively, they are called "devas" because they should be venerated;
this is the meaning of *deva*.
First, as for the hells:
twenty thousand yojanas beneath Jambudvīpa,
they extend twenty thousand yojanas across the four directions in a vast expanse.
It is composed entirely of pure iron;
its flames blaze intensely, and there are eight hot hells.
The first is called Saṃjīva (Reviving).
The second is called Black Rope;
the third, Crushing Multitude;
and the fourth, Screaming.
The fifth is Raurava (Great Wailing);
the sixth is Tapana (Scorching Heat);
the seventh is Pratāpana (Great Scorching Heat).
The eighth is the Avīci [Hell]. As for the Saṃjīva Hell:
sentient beings born there, impelled by their past karma, seize various weapons and give rise to mutual enmity and hatred.
They hack and strike one another until their bodies fall apart in pieces;
they faint and die for a moment,
but through a voice from the air, they are restored to life.
Even though those sentient beings are revived, they continue to hack and harm one another.
As for their lifespan:
the duration of one lifetime in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings constitutes a single day and night [for them].
Thus, by such calculation, their lifespan is five hundred years.
As for those who undergo these torments in the Black Rope Hell,
its wardens and the like—
Within the bodies of sentient beings, from the crown of the head to the feet,
they mark out boundaries and black lines, then dismember their limbs with flaming saws and axes;
by the power of their prior karma, they are dissolved and reborn in higher or lower realms.
Regarding their lifespan:
one lifetime-period of the Trāyastriṃśa gods constitutes a single day and night;
by such calculation, their lifespan is one thousand years.
Regarding the Saṃghāta Hell:
when sentient beings are born there,
they are struck with iron hammers or [crushed] between two iron mountains.
It is like two mountains with the heads of sheep coming together, grinding and crushing one another until they are destroyed;
when the two mountains part, fire spontaneously breaks out again,
and they are once more crushed to ruin.
Regarding their lifespan:
one lifetime of the Yāma devas constitutes a single day and night for those [devas].
Calculated in this manner, their lifespan is two thousand years.
As for the Hell of Wailing and Crying (*raurava*),
sentient beings born there,
out of fear of the hot iron pond, enter the dense forest.
Blazing with fierce flames, it burns perpetually.
By the power of their past karma, their tongues are a thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
There is a great ox there.
With iron horns and iron armor, they set up iron plowshares;
with blazing flames, they plow their tongues.
Such is their lifespan.
One lifetime in Tuṣita Heaven constitutes a single day and night [in this hell].
Calculated in this manner, their lifespan is four thousand years.
This is the Great Screaming Hell (Mahāraurava), where they undergo such agonizing suffering.
It is also the same as before;
their suffering is doubled.
As for their lifespan:
For the gods of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, one lifetime constitutes a single day and night;
by such calculation, their lifespan is eight thousand years.
Those who suffer such torments in the Saṃjīva (Reviving) Hell [endure this for that duration].
In the triple iron city, flames penetrate through to the very core, and beings therein undergo bitter suffering.
As for their lifespan:
one lifetime of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods constitutes a single day and night [for those beings].
Thus, their lifespan is sixteen thousand years.
Those who undergo such torments in the Hell of Utmost Heat are also the same as those previously described.
Their suffering increases manifold.
As for their lifespan,
it is equal to half an intermediate kalpa.
Regarding those who undergo such torment in the Avīci Hell:
within an iron chamber, their single body becomes a mass of flames as they experience extreme suffering.
As for their lifespan:
Regarding the sixteen *kalpas* of increase within the hells during one intermediate *kalpa*:
on each of the four sides of the eight hot hells, there are four secondary locations.
The first is the *Kukūla* (the Pit of Hot Ashes).
The depths all reach above the knees.
When sentient beings wander there,
as soon as they set foot down, [the ground sinks].
The skin, flesh, and blood are all scorched and sloughed off until only the bones remain;
yet as soon as they lift their feet, it grows back again.
It was restored to its original state.
However, the filth in the two gates increased,
and impure mud submerged the waists of sentient beings.
Within it, there are many *kṛmivaktra* insects whose beaks are as sharp as needles; they pierce the skin and penetrate the bone to suck and eat its marrow.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of *triśūla-śastra-vardhana*.
The Path of Sword Blades:
This refers to a great road spread out with sword blades facing upward,
upon which sentient beings must travel.
As soon as they set foot down,
their skin, flesh, and blood are all severed and crushed;
when they lift their feet, these are restored to life once more.
It recovers to its original state.
Second is the Forest of Sword Leaves;
this refers to a forest whose trees have exclusively sharp, keen swords and blades for leaves.
Sentient beings wander there;
when the wind blows, leaves fall and mangle their limbs, causing their flesh and bones to scatter.
There are brindled dogs that tear and drag them away to devour them.
The third is the Forest of Iron Thorns,
named *Tīkṣṇa-mālī*.
This refers to the trees in this forest which possess sharp iron thorns.
The thorns are sixteen finger-widths long;
when sentient beings are driven up and down the tree,
those sharp and piercing thorns stab them as they ascend and descend.
The flesh, blood, skin, and so forth of these sentient beings hang smeared upon the thorns until only their sinews and bones remain; there,
iron-beaked crows [peck at them].
They peck and probe at the eyes and brains of sentient beings,
vying with one another to devour them;
although the three types of paths, such as the Path of Sword Blades, differ from one another, the iron weapons used therein are the same.
Thus, one *ūṣmagata* encompasses four;
the *ūṣmagata* of the Fierce River is named "The Unfordable."
The cauldron is filled to the brim with intensely boiling lye-water;
sentient beings enter it,
sometimes floating and sometimes sinking.
Whether inverted or upright,
whether horizontal or vertical,
they are steamed and boiled until their flesh and bones are reduced to a pulp.
It is like a large cauldron filled with lye into which rice and other grains are placed;
as a fierce fire burns beneath it, the grains swirl up and down within, their entire bodies becoming completely disintegrated.
Sentient beings are likewise;
even if they wish to escape,
there are various hell-wardens upon both banks.
Holding swords and spears, they ward off [the offenders] and force them to turn back;
there is no way for them to escape.
This river is like a moat.
The first three resemble gardens.
Those are called the neighboring hells (*utsada-naraka*). Regarding the eight cold hells:
the first is called Arbuda (the Blister).
The second is called "Bubbling and Bursting";
the third is Aṭaṭa;
the fourth is Apapa.
Five: *Utkūla* (Choking Throat); Six:
*Kumuda* (Split like the *kumuda* flower, which is translated as "blue lotus"); Seven: *Padma* (Split like the lotus flower);
Eight: *Mahāpadma* (Split like the great lotus flower). ○ Regarding the *Arbuda* Hell (Blister Hell):
Born amidst the Cold Ice [Hell], where the extreme cold is most severe, blisters arise upon the body;
this is called the Water Blister Hell.
As for its lifespan:
If one were to remove a single sesame seed every hundred years from eighty *droṇas* of sesame seeds— the standard measure of Magadha— until they were all exhausted,
such would be the lifespan [of those in the Sañjīva hell]. As for the Pratāpana (Blazing) hell:
Due to the extreme cold,
those blisters burst and yellow fluid leaks out;
such is their lifespan.
The Aṭaṭa hell, which is twenty times greater than the former,
is so named because its inhabitants endure the biting of their teeth due to the intense cold.
As for its lifespan:
Twice as long as the preceding twenty [eons] is the lifespan of those in the A-pa-po (Ābaba) Hell,
where they endure the sounds of cold.
As for their life span:
Twice as much as the previous twenty [kalpas] is the duration of the "Vomit-throat" hell;
those who cry out due to cold produce this sound of suffering.
As for their lifespan:
The hell-beings of the *Utpala* Hell, where the body splits twenty times more than before like an *utpala* flower,
have their bodies split like the petals of an *utpala* flower due to the severe cold;
such is their lifespan.
As for those in the Lotus-Cleft Hell, which is twenty times more severe than the former,
their bodies split open like blooming lotuses due to the intense cold.
As for their lifespan:
As for those in the Hell of the Twenty-fold Great Lotus Splitting,
their bodies are split more extensively than before,
like a great lotus flower in full bloom with many petals.
As for their lifespan,
it is double that of the former twenty;
as for the hell of the solitary ones:
In the mountain wildernesses of Jambudvīpa,
one experiences suffering and pleasure for a single day and night;
because these are experienced in alternation, there are the eight hot hells and the eight cold hells, along with the neighboring, isolated, and solitary hells.
These are called the eighteen hells.
Regarding the two types of hungry ghosts:
five hundred yojanas beneath the city of Rājagṛha, there is a city of hungry ghosts.
It is called Yellow-White,
and it is also called Pale and Dismal.
The king of ghosts there is named King Yama, the Dharma King.
They dwell together with thirty-six retinues and the like;
there are four such categories.
The first is external obstruction (*bāhyāvaraṇa*).
Second, internal obstacles;
third, obstacles regarding food and drink;
fourth, obstacles to food and drink.
First, the external obstruction:
one cannot even hear the sounds of food and drink.
Second, the internal obstruction:
Even if they obtain a small amount of food and drink, their mouths are like the eye of a needle, unable to admit it;
even if it could enter the mouth, their throats are like horse-tails, unable to allow it to pass;
and even if it were to pass the throat, their bellies are like mountain caverns, unable to be filled.
Although their bellies are full, their legs are like blades of grass so that they are unable to move;
thus they undergo this great suffering.
Third is the obstacle of food and drink.
When they see food and drink,
immeasurable hell-wardens seize various weapons and guard it so that nothing can be obtained.
These are the four obstacles to food and drink.
When they eat food,
iron balls produced by their karma and molten copper poured into their mouths flow out from below.
These four types are all hungry ghosts (preta).
Regarding their lifespan:
one human month constitutes a single day and night;
calculated in this manner, their life span is five hundred years.
This corresponds to fifteen thousand years in the human realm. Or,
those who dwell in places such as the Cold Forest (Śītavana) and consume blood,
flesh, and the like are all of the class of hungry ghosts (preta).
Third, as for animals (*tiryagyoni*),
they mostly dwell in rivers and oceans,
living in dense masses like fermented grain dregs.
The large prey upon the small, and the small prey upon the large;
they terrify one another as they dwell amidst the waves and surges of the sea, which never remain still.
Or they may dwell among humans or devas;
as for their lifespan,
it is as long as that of a nāga king, lasting half an intermediate kalpa.
The shortest lifespan is that of a gnat and the like, lasting for a single kṣaṇa.
Their physical dimensions are not fixed.
As for the four types of persons:
They dwell in the four great continents, the eight intermediate continents, and various minor islands.
As for their lifespan,
it is like that of the people of Jambudvīpa.
At the beginning of the kalpa of formation, their lifespan was immeasurable;
subsequently, it gradually decreased until it is now sixty years.
Thereafter, the lifespan gradually decreases until it reaches ten years;
subsequently, it increases again without a fixed limit.
In Uttarakuru, the people have a fixed lifespan of one thousand years.
The people of Pūrvavideha have a lifespan of five hundred years;
the people of Aparagoyānī have a lifespan of two hundred and fifty years;
and except for Uttarakuru, there are premature deaths and untimely calamities elsewhere.
They enjoy these things; in Uttarakuru,
food consists of naturally growing rice,
and clothing and ornaments emerge from wish-fulfilling trees.
Regarding the other three continents,
they subsist on food such as grain and meat, and enjoy various treasures and resources.
Their physical stature is four cubits, equal to that of the people of Jambudvīpa.
The inhabitants of Pūrvavideha in the east are eight cubits in height;
those of Aparagoyānī in the west are sixteen cubits;
and those of Uttarakuru in the north are thirty-two cubits.
The facial features of the people there are also shaped like those of the continents;
the people of the small sub-continents are likewise like those of the great continents,
though their bodies are each reduced by half in size.
Therefore, it is said thus:
the five classes of non-gods (asura) dwell beneath the water-level of Mount Sumeru.
Beyond eleven thousand yojanas,
within the city of Jyotiṣprabha in the vast expanse of the mountains,
resides the Asura King Rāhu— here translated as "Seizer of the Brain"— together with his retinue.
Furthermore, after passing ten thousand one hundred yojanas,
within the city of Tārāmālā dwells an asura king named Śikhaṇḍamālā.
It is inhabited by a multitude of kinsmen.
Furthermore, beyond eleven thousand yojanas lies the city of Dṛḍhā, where the Asura King resides.
It is named Wondrous Stability;
it is also called Great Power,
where a multitude of retinues reside.
Furthermore, ten thousand one hundred yojanas beyond,
within the exceedingly deep city,
dwells the asura king named Vemacitra— translated here as "Various Silks" or "Variegated Body"— together with his retinue.
They constantly engage in rivalry and conflict with Śakra.
Their city is called Suvarṇaka (Possessing Gold),
and their palace is named Saṃgītī (Music).
The king of wish-fulfilling trees is named Tāmbūla,
and the place where they gather is called Bhadra-dhana.
The stone is named Good Virtue;
the garden is named Universal Joy;
[the lands are] Wondrous Joy, Supreme Joy, Exceeding Joy, and Good Ground.
He is also named Universal Joy, Wondrous Joy, Supreme Joy, and Utmost Joy.
The elephant he rides when facing battle is named Invincible;
the elephant he rides for his pastimes is named Snowy Mound.
The horse is said to have a "steep neck.
These beings, together with the Thirty-three Heavens, contend for the flavor of *sūdāma* and for the women of the asuras; because of this strife, they emerge from the mountain ranges.
His body was clad in firm armor made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and white jade;
in his hands he held swords, spears, javelins, lances, bows, and arrows,
leading an army of four divisions.
That Asura King Rāhu [wore] a neck-garland and exquisite pendants.
Vemacitrin and the others—
either the first three arrive,
or all four arrive.
At that time, Śakra’s five protective hosts returned:
first, the assembly led by the Nāga King Sukhābhirata, who dwells in the Playful Ocean, returned from their battle against the armies of the asuras.
If the nāgas do not prevail, they withdraw to the place of Firm Resolve (Dṛḍhavīrya) and,
together with the two guardians, again engage in battle with the asuras.
If they do not prevail there either, they withdraw to the place of Wreath-Bearers (Mālādharas).
Together with three guardians, they again engaged in battle.
Furthermore, if they were not victorious, they went to the place of the *hṛda* (heart-mantras).
Together with four guardians, they again engaged in battle.
Furthermore, if they cannot prevail and go to the abode of the Four Great Kings,
where they again engage in battle with the five guardians;
then the Four Great Heavenly Kings lead their fourfold armies.
Clad in precious, firm armor and wielding various spears and staves in battle,
the Four Heavenly Kings are for the most part victorious;
yet they cannot repel the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
They spoke first to Śakra, saying, "We are unable to turn back that Asura King through our protection; you yourself must repel the enemy.
Having spoken thus, they [departed].
The Lord of Devas, Śakra, riding upon the elephant Supratiṣṭhita,
addressed the assembly of the Thirty-three Gods, saying:
"You should all know this."
"Now that the army of the asuras has reached the summit of Mount Sumeru,
you must don sturdy armor, take up your vehicle, and engage the asuras in battle.
Having spoken these words, [he departed].
Those devaputras each donned precious armor and grasped spears and weapons;
departing from the Garden of Many Chariots, they took their respective vehicles and entered the Garden of Coarse Evil,
where both body and mind became increasingly depraved.
They emerge from the city of Sudarśana to wage war against the asuras.
If the asuras are victorious, they invade as far as within the city;
if the devas are victorious, they pursue the asura army as far as the First Sea.
During the time of battle,
when the devas and asuras sever their necks or waists,
they die immediately.
If their hands or feet were severed,
they would grow back as they were before.
This occurs when a Bhagavān, a Pratyekabuddha, or a Cakravartin King dwells in the world.
The asuras do not give rise to a contentious mind.
Even if they should hold their ground, the devas will surely be victorious;
as worldly goodness increases, the host of devas shall also prevail.
When unwholesome states increase in the world, the asuras prevail;
therefore, the devas protect and uphold wholesome matters.
As for the six classes of devas:
The six heavens of the desire realm,
the seventeen of the form realm,
and the four of the formless realm.
Regarding the six heavens of the desire realm:
on the first tier of Mount Sumeru dwell the hosts of Kṛtātmā;
on the second tier dwell the hosts of Mālādharā.
On the third level, the city named Anāgāpātī is located on the northern side of Mount Yugandhara,
where the gods of the Nityapramuditā class reside.
The yakṣa hosts of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa dwell there.
Thus, in the east is the city named Bhadrauttara,
where there is a great heavenly king.
His name is Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
the hosts of Gandharvas dwell there.
To the west, there is a city.
It is named Various Colors.
There is a great celestial king there named Wide-Eyed.
The assembly of nāga deities resides there.
To the south, there is a city named Vardhana.
There is a Great Heavenly King named Virūḍhaka,
whose retinue of Jyotiṣka-dhvajas dwells there.
On the other four tiers dwell the Seven Golden Mountains, the sun, moon, and stars, the Cakravāḍa mountains, the mountains of Jambudvīpa, the Tāla trees, and the hosts of the Four Great Kings.
All belong to the Four Great Kings;
this is called one class.
As for their lifespan:
Fifty human years constitute one day and night for them;
thus their lifespan extends for five hundred such years.
Their physical stature is one-quarter of a krośa.

On the summit of Mount Sumeru, in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, dwells in the most excellent abode together with the asura maidens known as the "Beautifully Peaceful" (Miaonan). There,
he enjoys various sensual pleasures alongside the host of celestial maidens, never feeling satiated.
Furthermore, there was an elephant king upon whom he rode when facing battle,
named Suvihita; this was the same elephant king upon whom he rode while sporting in the pleasure groves.
They are named Airāvaṇa, which here means "Son of the Earth-Sustainer. Two elephants surround them, each seven yojanas in circumference, with eight thousand small elephants dwelling in each group.
Furthermore, there is a horse king.
He is named Swift Wind;
he dwells with eight thousand horses,
and his ministers, the counselors of the Lord of Devas, number thirty-two.
For this reason, they are called the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
When the sons of gods become heedless, they become addicted to the pleasures of the five desires.
There is a great celestial drum;
from its sound issues a voice that warns the devas, saying:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent."
All that is tainted is suffering;
all phenomena are without self;
cessation is bliss.
When engaged in battle with the armies of the asuras,
he uttered a cry that dispels suffering, warning them:
"May the devas be victorious!"
May the defeat of the asuras,
their palaces, cities, walls, trees, and gathered rocks,
be as previously explained.
Regarding the lifespan of those devas:
one hundred human years constitutes a single day and night for them;
by such calculation, their lifespan is ten years.
The stature of those celestial beings is half a yojana.
As for the Yāma devas, they contend with the Trāyastriṃśa devas and the asuras;
because they are free from such contention, they are called the "Devas Free from Contention" (Yāma).
As for the lifespan of those devas,
two hundred human years constitute one day and night;
by such calculation, their lifespan is two thousand years.
The stature of those devas is two yojanas. As for the Tuṣita Heaven,
there resides the Honored One Maitreya,
who shall succeed to both the mundane and supramundane realms.
The station of the Dharma King, where one experiences the great joy of the Dharma,
is called Tuṣita;
this signifies the meaning of "all-joy."
Four hundred years among humans constitute one day and night for that deva;
their lifespan is four thousand such years.
The body size is four yojanas. As for the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati), they delight in emanations because they themselves create and enjoy [objects of pleasure];
thus it is called "Delighting in Emanations."
Eight hundred years among humans is one day and night in that heaven;
their lifespan is eight thousand years.
Their body size is eight yojanas. As for the Paranirmita-vaśavartin [Heaven], they enjoy the transformations created by others;
thus it is called Paranirmita-vaśavartin.
The sovereign of that heaven possesses majestic power and autonomy;
this constitutes one day and night for that deity, which is equivalent to sixteen hundred years among humans for the Lord of Māra.
Their lifespan is sixteen thousand years,
and their bodies are sixteen yojanas in height.
From the Avīci Hell below up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven above, [this is the extent of the realm].
This is called the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
It is so described because its inhabitants are addicted to sensual pleasures and consume edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
Regarding the seventeen heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*): [text continues].
Regarding the inclusion within the four dhyānas: as for the three heavens of the first dhyāna,
they are the Brahmakāyika, the Brahmapurohita, and [the Mahābrahmā].
Mahābrahmā,
the lifespan of those devas is half an eon for the Brahmakāyika gods.
The Brahmā-purohita [heaven] lasts for one kalpa;
the Mahābrahmā [heaven] lasts for one and a half kalpas.
Such is the sequence of the physical dimensions of those devas.
Half a yojana, one yojana,
and one and a half yojanas. Regarding the three heavens of the second dhyāna:
Namely, Limited Light,
Immeasurable Light,
and Utmost Light.
Regarding the lifespan of those devas:
for the Heaven of Limited Light, it is two kalpas;
for the four higher heavens, forty intermediate kalpas constitute one great kalpa.
From the gods below,
eighty intermediate kalpas constitute one great kalpa: four kalpas for the Heaven of Immeasurable Light,
and eight kalpas for the Heaven of Utmost Light-Purity.
The bodies of those devas are two *yojanas* in height; their light is two *yojanas* for those of Limited Light (*Parīttābha*) and four *yojanas* for those of Immeasurable Light (*Apramāṇābha*).
For those of Utmost Light (*Ābhāsvara*), it is eight *yojanas*. Regarding the three heavens of the Third Dhyāna, they are called "Limited Virtue" (*Parīttaśubha*).
Immeasurable goodness,
vast goodness;
such is the lifespan of those devas.
Minor goodness for sixteen kalpas;
immeasurable goodness for thirty-two kalpas;
extensive goodness for sixty-four kalpas.
As for the body size of those devas:
those with minor merit are sixteen yojanas tall;
those with immeasurable merit are thirty-two yojanas tall.
The Vast Virtue [Heaven] is sixty-four yojanas [in extent]. Regarding the eight heavens of the Fourth Dhyāna:
Anabhraka (Cloudless), Puṇyaprasava (Merit-Born), and so forth.
The Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala),
the Third Dhyāna abode of ordinary beings,
and the Unafflicted (Avṛha).
Avīci, Sudarśana, and Sudṛśa.
Akaniṣṭha. These five are the abodes of the noble ones,
known as the Five Pure Abodes (pañca śuddhāvāsāḥ).
The lifespan of those gods is one hundred and twenty-five kalpas in the Cloudless Heaven,
and two hundred and fifty kalpas in the Heaven of Merit-Born.
Five hundred kalpas for the Bṛhatphala heaven;
one thousand kalpas for the Avṛha heaven;
two thousand kalpas for the Atapa heaven.
In Sudarśana it is four thousand kalpas;
in Sudṛśa, eight thousand kalpas;
and in Akaniṣṭha, sixteen thousand kalpas.
As for the body size of those devas:
in the Anabhraka heaven it is one hundred and twenty-five yojanas;
in the Puṇyaprasava heaven, it is two hundred and fifty yojanas.
The Bṛhatphala heaven is five hundred yojanas;
the Avṛha heaven is one thousand yojanas;
the Atapa heaven is two thousand yojanas.
Sudṛśā is four thousand yojanas;
Sudarśana is eight thousand yojanas;
