then spring will entirely enter summer,
and the seasons will become completely disordered.
If the intercalary month is lost twelve times in succession,
the *zi* hour will all enter the *chou* branch;
thus, the year will not be formed at all.
The Master Zhongyong of the Three Sovereigns said:
"Sovereign" (Huang) means great.
Within and without, there is non-action.
This refers to those who transform the people through the Way.
Lei Shi says that the remote antiquity of the vast wilderness began with the Three Sovereigns:
Fuxi, Nong, and Xuanyuan. First was Taohao Fuxi, whose surname was Feng.
He was titled Taohao.
His mother was named Huaxu;
she conceived him after treading upon the footprint of a giant.
With the body of a serpent and the head of a human,
they raised sacrificial victims for their kitchens.
It is also said:
Pao Xi (Fuxi).
An Guo was the first to designate him as a king;
his posthumous title was Jingmin (Tranquil People).
The Record of the Law states: Huang, who embodied the virtue of wood, resided in Chenliu and governed the borders of Xiaohuang County in Yanzhou for one hundred and ten years;
it was he who first drew the eight trigrams.

They created writing and seals to replace the system of knotted cords; from this, literature and records arose. They established the rites of marriage: when a woman is given away, it is called "marrying her off" (jia); when a man takes a wife, it is called "wedding" (qu). They set out nets and snares to catch fish; these were fishing nets and bird-cages.
In the *Erya*, bird traps are called *luo*;
fish traps are called *quan*; and rabbit traps are called *zhi*.
A *se* lute has twenty-five strings, is seven feet two inches long, and one foot eight inches wide; its progenitor was the matriarch Fuxi, whose surname was Feng.
She was the younger sister of Fuxi.
She was able to transform all things; she fashioned the *sheng* reed organ, four chi in length, by arranging tubes within a gourd shell and applying the reeds.
The larger has nineteen reeds and the smaller has thirteen reeds.
The bamboo stem is thirty-seven [units] long,
and each reed is four chi and two cun in length.
He used bamboo for this purpose;
its shapes were jagged like bird feathers. He smelted stones of five colors to mend the deficiency of heaven and severed the legs of a giant turtle to establish the four cardinal points.
He reigned for one hundred and forty years.

[The following were the successive sovereigns: Gonggong, Datingshi, Bohuangshi, Zhongyangshi, Lulishi, Lilianshi, Xuxushi, Zunlushi, Hunchunshi, Haoyingshi, Getianshi, Zhuxiangshi, Yinkangshi, and Wuhuaishi.
In total, there were fifteen generations spanning seventeen thousand seven hundred and eighty-seven years;
these are not recorded in the Classics or Histories.
9. The Earth God. Formerly, Gonggong had a son named Houtu, who was able to level the Nine Provinces.
The sacrifice is for the deity of the she (she-shen),
the lord of the five types of soil.
These five types of soil refer to mountains, rivers, marshes, hills, mounds, plains, and low-lying wetlands.
The soil is distant, vast, and moist; one sacrifices to the mound of earth to repay the labors of the soil.
It is unknown in which generation it was paired with Hou-tu (the Lord of the Soil);
this remains to await those who may know.
10. Yan Di Shennong Shi was of the Jiang clan.
His title was Yan Di Mu Deng Shi.
He was born through the inspiration of a divine dragon.
His human body had the head of an ox;
he grew up by the Jiang River, and thus it became his surname. His dynasty was based on the virtue of fire.
He moved the capital from Duchen to Quwo.
He reigned for one hundred and forty years and was buried at Changsha.
The *I Ching* says:
"Shennong carved wood to make the plowshare."
He fashioned the plow from supple wood and first taught the world how to sow the five grains.
He further tasted a hundred flavors to compose the "Pharmacopoeia" for treating illnesses with medicine, and he expanded the eight trigrams into sixty-four.
They engaged in market commerce and trade;
they performed sacrifices and prepared the five-stringed lute,
which symbolizes the Five Elements.
From Zixia to Dichi, Chengdi, Lindi, Kuīdi, Mìngdi, Zhìdi, Lái Di, Āidi,
and Yúwǎng— altogether eight generations for five hundred and forty years.
11. Dinghai: Huangdi of Youxiong, surnamed Gongsun and named Xuanyuan, was the second son of Shaodian.
He was born with divine and spiritual qualities.
Though weak, he was able to speak;
though young, he followed the rules of propriety;
as he grew, he became earnest and quick-witted.
He was accomplished and possessed of great intelligence.
Toward the end of the Yu-gang era, the feudal lords attacked one another;
the Emperor fashioned the bow and arrow to subdue them.
The whole world submitted.
On Mount Xinban, he subdued tigers, leopards, bears, and wolves;
there were the eighty-one brothers of Chiyou, with copper heads and iron foreheads.
Eating sand and swallowing stones—
these are the essences of the mountains and seas that bring chaos to the world.
He fought on the plains of Zhuolu and received the mandate of execution from the Central Emperor;
he cast the cauldrons and became a flying immortal.
He ascended the dragon and departed.
He lived for two hundred and ten years.
His robes and cap were buried at Mount Qiao; he had occupied the throne for one hundred years.
His minister, Zu Che, carved wood to create the first images of ministers.
He led the feudal lords in court for ten years, established the administration, constructed the Hall of Harmony (Hegong), and fashioned clothing.
He commissioned Lu Ban to build boats and chariots; the boat is that which glides upon the water.
It can be used to ferry across water;
it serves as a carriage-shed.
It can be used for traveling or dwelling, for erecting houses and buildings, and for fashioning inner and outer coffins to escort the deceased.
The funeral rites first began; the Rites state:
"For the Son of Heaven, the body is encoffined after seven days and buried after seven months."
The feudal lords were encoffined on the fifth day;
they were buried in the fifth month.
This applied to Great Officers, as well as ordinary officers and commoners.
The encoffining takes place on the third day;
the burial takes place after three months.
The mound for a Son of Heaven is three fathoms high.
They plant pine trees;
for the feudal lords, they plant half as many.
They plant cypress trees.
For a Great Officer, the height is eight chi;
it is planted with chestnut trees.
For an officer of the appropriate rank, the height is four chi.
They plant huai trees [at the graves of] commoners. Commoners have no mounds;
they plant willows and poplars.
He performed the Xianchi music, employing Tian Lao, Li Mu, and Taishan Ji as his ministers.

On the first day of the month of Jiazi—[the first of the ten stems]—Feng Hou established the Jiazi cycle (one source says Da Nao did so). This was the thirty-eighth year since the Emperor ascended the throne.
He first commanded Daonao to create the sexagenary cycle beginning with Jiazi;
thus, the thirty-eighth year was established as the first Jiazi.
By retroactively calculating from this, the first year of the era was found to be the year Dinghai. Rongcheng devised the calendar and Lishou developed the art of calculation.
He questioned Guangchengzi;
Cangjie served as the Recorder;
Qibo distinguished the medicinal herbs.
Yu Fu established the *Mingjing* (Classic of Pulse);
Ling Lun fashioned the pitch-pipes and musical scales to harmonize the tones.
The pipes were nine inches long and made of bamboo.
Whether causing harm or benefit, the five musical tones were established based on this; as recorded in the *Lì dì jì* (Annals of the Emperors) concerning the nine provinces:
"The Yellow Emperor had twenty-five sons."
Twelve individuals obtained surnames:
Ji, You, Qi, Yi, Teng, Zhen, Ren, Xun, Xi, Shi, Xuan, and Xiu;
they divided the governance of the Nine Provinces.
That is to say, Ji, Qing, Xu, Yu, Yong, Liang, Chu, Yang, Yan;
from the eldest to the youngest,
they were enfeoffed in this order.
Subsequently, the descendants of his lineage— the Five Emperors and the Three Kings—
were all his progeny.
The Emperor married a woman of the Datingshi clan and fathered two sons.
The eldest was named Xuānxiāo;
the youngest was named Chāngyì. Altogether there were eighteen generations, spanning one thousand five hundred and twenty years.
The Master Zhongyong of the Five Emperors said:
"The title 'Emperor' (Di) refers to the essential nature.
Inwardly, his mind is non-active, yet outwardly, his traces involve active engagement."
He governed the people through the transformation of virtue.
Virtue that mirrors Heaven and Earth is called "Di" (The Sovereign).
[The lineages] were known as Lei, Shaozhuan, Ku, Tang Yao, and Yu Shun, transmitted down to Xia.
12. Jiazi 2. Shao Hao of the Jintian Clan: his surname was Yi, his given name was Zhi, and his courtesy name was Qingyang;
his mother was named Nüjie.
There was a star like a rainbow that descended and flowed away;
[the child] was born through its spiritual influence.
He had disheveled hair and went barefoot, wearing neither crown nor cap.
The son of the Yellow Emperor lived for one hundred years; he ascended the throne in the year Dingmao.
He reigned for eighty-four years.
His personal name was Jinde.
He moved the capital to Qiong Sang and later to Qufu,
where he established wards and markets.
He established one hundred and twenty musical troupes for ceremonial performances and used birds to designate official ranks; subsequently,
the phoenix arrived.
In total, there were ten generations spanning four hundred and ninety years.
Thirteen. Jiazi Year 3. 3. Zhuanxu Gaoyang, whose surname was Ji.
His name was Zhuanxu.
He was the grandson of the Yellow Emperor and the son of Changyi.
There was a star like a rainbow;
a woman was moved by it and gave birth [to him].
He lived to the age of ninety-eight before his demise.
He was buried at Dunqiu; his inscriptions and correspondence were recorded as having been established in the year Xinmao.
He occupied the throne for seventy-eight years.
His reign was characterized by the virtue of Water.
The capital was Diqiu, located at the present-day city of Puyang; he established the calendar with the beginning of the first month of spring as its epoch.
He fashioned a flat-crowned cap (*pingguanmian*) eight inches wide and one foot six inches long.
Reaching the Zhou dynasty, the regulation of the *liu* (pendants) first began;
there were twelve each at the front and back, using *zǎo* and jade ornaments,
with twenty-four officials in charge of the nine ranks and three grades of ceremonies.
Nurturing materials according to their nature and assigning tasks according to the land;
bearing up with the times and emulating Heaven;
where the divine and the human are not intermingled.
All things were established in their proper order.
He gave birth to eight talented sons known as the Eight Kai,
who quelled the rebellion of the Nine Li.
He regulated the vital breaths through transformation and instruction;
he purified his sincerity for sacrifices;
and he distinguished the way between ruler and subject.
The creation of the music of five stems was intended to harmonize with the foundation of the Five Elements. In total, there were eight dynasties spanning five hundred and twenty years.
14. Jiazi Year. Fourth: Emperor Ku (Gaoxin), whose surname was Ji.
His name was Qi.
He was the great-grandson of the Yellow Emperor and the grandson of Xuanyiao.
Qiao Xuanzi passed away at the age of one hundred five;
he was buried in Yiyang on a Jisi day. A stele was erected there.
He reigned for seventy-nine years.
The king possessed the virtue of wood.
His capital was Bo, located at present-day Yan Shi County; his personal name was Shichong.
Songzi appointed the officials of the Five Elements: Goumang, the son of Shaohao, as the Minister of Wood;

Zhurong, the son of Zhuanxu, as the Minister of Fire; Rufou, the son of Zhuanxu, as the Minister of Metal; Xuanming, also a son of Shaohao, as the Minister of Water; and Houtu, the son of Gaoyang, as the Minister of Earth. From Gaoyang’s son were born the Eight Talented Sons.
These were called the Eight Yuans.
They fashioned cauldrons, tripods, *wei*, drums, bells, stone chimes, ocarinas, and flutes; they joined wood with leather to make drums, which resounded only when struck.
The *zhong* is cast from refined metal or molded from clay;
it resembles a bell but is not circular.
It is two feet and two and a half inches in height.
It is eight *fen* thick and is called a suspended bell (*xuánzhōng*).
The stone chime (*qìng*) is three *lǜ* and two feet seven inches long at its front.
The latter is two *chi* long and one foot eight inches wide;
it is named Huangzhong.
The *qing* and *xuan* are made by firing clay.
It is as large as a wild goose egg;
it is pointed at the top and flat at the bottom, with five holes.
The *Baibutong* says:
Its shape is like that of a scale weight and it has six holes;
this differs slightly from the *Zhouli*.
The *chi* is made of bamboo.
It is one chi and four cun in height and three cun in circumference;
the smaller version is one chi and two cun.
It has six holes at the top, making nine openings in total. This is the ninth generation.
Three hundred and fifty years later,
the *Zuozhuan* states: "Cangshu, Tuiyi, Taoyin,
Dalin, Pangjiang, Tingjian, Zhongrong, and Shudada."
These are called the Eight Kai:
Bo Fen, Zhong Kan, Shu Xian, Shu Bao, Ji Zhong, Bo Hu, Zhong Xiong, and Li Li; these are called the Eight Yuan.
15. Jiazi. 5. Emperor Yao of the Táo Dáng clan, surnamed Qí.
His name was Fangxun.
He was the great-grandson of the Yellow Emperor and the second son of Emperor Ku.
He was born after fourteen months of gestation.
His eyebrows were divided by eight-colored streaks.
He established his reign in the year Jiachen, dwelling in thatched huts upon earthen steps.
He reigned for ninety-eight years.
The king’s virtue was Fire.
He made Pingyang—present-day Jinzhou—his capital, and later moved it to An-yi.
Shun governed for one hundred and eighteen years,
beginning in the year Bingyin and ending in Gui-mao. He observed the mourning period for two years until Bisi,
when he passed away at the age of one hundred and eighty.
He was buried at Gulin.
His posthumous title was "Wing-Shan Chuan-Sheng" (One Who Transmits the Sage through Virtuous Conduct), his honorific name was Yao, and his era name was Zai.
He was the teacher of Master Ju-ying.
He charged Xi and He to observe the calendar and the movements of the sun, moon, stars, and constellations,
reverently transmitting the seasons to the people.
Heaven sent down a ewe named Chu-xie (Corrupter).
To the right of the tomb,
a mingejiao (calendula) plant grew,
reaching a height of eight chi.
On the first day of the month, one leaf grows;
by the full moon, all fifteen leaves are complete;
after the full moon, one leaf withers.
When the year ended and all things had withered away,
there was a lamb named Xièzhài (Rhinoceros) that died and was buried to the left of the hall.
The *zhucǎo* (vermilion grass) grew to a height of one zhang;

it was called the "grass that points out the sycophant. He established the *héngshì* (balcony chamber), constructed a chessboard with three hundred and sixty lines to represent the thirty-six decans (*xiún*), and instructed Danzhu [in its use].
He also composed great musical pieces.
Rice grew in profusion and phoenixes arrived.

There were thirty-two men of virtue whose names and surnames are unknown; [the Emperor] set up a "Drum for Bold Remonstrance. When the Great Flood lasted for nine years, he commissioned Gùn and then Yù to manage it; on the tenth day, ten suns appeared simultaneously, so he commanded Yì to shoot them down.
Nine birds fell dead upon the ground.
According to the Confucian accounts, there is a country in the southeast called Xiyanguo (the Land of Xihé).
There was a woman there named Xihé.
Ten days after his birth, he was bathed in the sea.
At that time, ten suns appeared simultaneously;
Houyi shot down nine of them.
Only this remains. Zhang Yi was a man skilled at archery.
He once obtained the medicine of immortality from the Queen Mother of the West;
it was a "beast-zhi" (animal fungus).
His wife stole and ate it;
she fled into the Moon Palace,
where she was named Cháng'ē.
For this reason, the moon is named the Toad;
it is simply the "farmer of the fields" (田父).
16. Jiazi. 6. Emperor Shun of the Yuyi clan had the surname Yao.
His name was Zhonghua;
his courtesy name was Dujun.
He was the sixth-generation descendant of Zhuanxu.
He had the countenance of a dragon and large lips;
his eyes possessed double pupils.
At the age of twenty, he became renowned throughout the world for his filial piety.
At thirty, he ascended the throne and toured the south.
He passed away at Cangwu at the age of one hundred and fifty. His reign was characterized by the virtue of Earth.
He resided at Dupo (present-day Hezhong Prefecture). During the time of Yao, he served as regent for twenty-eight years.
In total, he governed for fifty years; he ascended the throne in the year Bingwu and passed away in Yiwei.
He was buried at Mount Jiuyi.
He was posthumously titled Renshenghuiming (Benevolent, Sage, Kind, and Enlightened) and called Shun; he sang the "Nanfeng" (South Wind) poem.
He appointed the sixteen ministers—referring to the eight Kai and the eight Yuan—and banished the four villains. The *Zuozhuan* states:
"Huanxiong was a son of the Yellow Emperor."
A man of no talent;
he conceals righteousness and hides virtue,
delighting in the practice of cruelty and violence.
They are called Hündun and Gonggong;
these were the unworthy sons of Shao Hao.
One who destroys trust, abandons loyalty,
and exalts ornate evil speech is called Qiongqi;
such was Goujian under Zhuanxu.
He is a man of no talent;
arrogant and defiant toward those of illustrious virtue,
he brings disorder to the eternal laws of Heaven.
This refers to the "Praying Mechanism of the Three Miao.
The descendant of the Yellow Emperor’s minister, the Jinyun Clan,
was an unworthy son who was greedy for food and drink.
To be greedy for wealth and profit is called being a "taotuo.
When the minister Chui was making lacquerware, the Emperor said:
It is said that Gao Yao adjudicated lawsuits and established the five punishments; the Book states:
"The five punishments originated in the era of Shun.
This is the commentary by Zheng.
The *Liji* says:
"Mozi [taught] that one should scarify the forehead and stain it with ink,
except when entering or leaving on official business."
Those who do not act according to the Way and righteousness are subjected to this:
"Nose-cutting" means the removal of the nose.
Those who altered their carriages, robes, or changed the established regulations were subjected to this;
"fei" refers to the amputation of the feet.
"Breaking through barriers and canals, and leaping over city walls—
this is what is added [to the punishment].
'Palace' refers to men having their virility removed and women being confined in dark chambers."
If men and women engage in sexual intercourse without the observance of ritual propriety and righteousness,
this [punishment] shall be applied;
"great execution" refers to the death penalty.
Regarding those who plunder as bandits, apply this [punishment] to them.
To perform the Shao music and construct the Zongzhang Hall: the Shao consists of nine numbers and eleven [elements];
there are six musical pieces on the hall.
The *zhù* is like a lacquered wooden barrel;
it is two chi and four cun square and one chi and eight cun deep.
Inside it is a mallet handle;
with this, one produces music.
The *yu* resembles a crouching tiger.
On its back are twenty-four notches,
carved with pieces of wood about one chi in length;
this follows the principle of the ultimate number of the three nines of the Yang.
It was struck to bring the music to a halt.
The zither is three chi and six cun long,
symbolizing the three hundred and sixty days of the year.
It is six inches wide,
symbolizing the six directions of the universe.
At its top is an opening called the "pool."
The lower opening is called Bin;
it is wide in the front and narrow in the back,
symbolizing the distinction between the honorable and the humble.
It is circular at the top and square at the bottom,
following the pattern of heaven and earth;
it has seven strings made of refined red silk.
It is seven chi and two cun in length.
This accords with the seventy-two seasonal signs (*qiuhou*).
There is a saying:
King Wen and King Wu of Zhou added two strings to the five-stringed zither to complete it as a seven-stringed instrument;
the large and small strings were used to harmonize the sentiments between ruler and minister.
The *Fengsu Tong* states:
"The qin is the sovereign of music;
the gentleman plays it without ever being separated from his person."
It is not like bells and drums set out in the ancestral temple or arranged upon the sounding-frames and stands;
for its size is moderate and its resonance is harmonious and elegant,
being neither so loud as to be clamorous and diffuse.
Though small, it is not extinguished and is not unheard;
it is sufficient to inspire the spirit and vigor of others.
"Ses" is as previously annotated.
The *bōfǔ* is shaped like a drum and made of leather;
it is stuffed with winnowing-rice husks.
One strikes it according to the rhythmic beat.
The musical instrument is the *qiúyù* (jade ball).
It is used to strike the *qìng* stone to cause it to ring out. There are five types of music performed in the hall below.
The *xiao* resembles the wings of a phoenix;
it is made by weaving bamboo strips together and measures one chi and five cun in length.
The large version consists of twenty-three tubes and is called the *diao-xiao*;
the small version consists of sixteen tubes and is called the *ya-xiao*.
According to the *Rites of Zhou* (*Zhouli*).
There are two types of *yā* flutes.
The *cháng* flute is one chi and four cun long and consists of twenty-four tubes; the *fán* flute is likewise.
The twenty-three-piped *guǎngxiāo* is one chi and two cun long;
it has a handle at its base for holding and shaking, with side-ears.
"Self-striking" refers to the *yong*, the large bell.
The *sheng* is as previously noted in the commentary.
The *guan* is made of bamboo.
It has seven apertures; twelve provinces were established.
For burials prior to Shao Hao, earthenware coffins were used.
The titles of the rulers throughout the world reflected their respective virtues.
Since the time of Zhuanxu,
the titles of the world have followed their personal names,
such as Gaoyang and Gaoxin.
These are all the lands where [the sages] arose.
The *Waiji* of the Liu clan regards the titles of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors as mere popular legends.
As for the Three Kings, the *Zhongyongzi* says:
The King went forth.
Furthermore, he supplemented his governance with punishments and defenses;
because his posthumous title was "Ren" (Benevolent) and he was one who proceeded according to righteousness, he is called a "King. This refers to the three dynasties of Xia, Shang, and Zhou.
Xia: Lei said: Yu, Qi, San, Kang, Xiang, Ning, Huai, Mang, Xie, Long, Ju, Jin, Jia, Gao, Fa, and Jie—these are the seventeen rulers.
[The total is] four hundred and thirty-two.
17. Jiǎzǐ 7: The Xiahou clan took the surname Sì. His name was Wénmìng, and his courtesy name was Gāodī;
he was the eighth-generation descendant of the Yellow Emperor.
The son of Gǔn was styled King Yù. Initially,
Shùn appointed Yù to manage the floodwaters.
He did not prize a foot-square jade disc but valued a moment of time.
He passed his own gate three times without entering.
Wang Jin’s virtue was such that he resided in Duan-yi (present-day Junzhou), and later moved to Qianyang Di; he served as the Minister of the Court of State Ceremonies under Yao.
Zheng’s Commentary:
The first is the Minister of Personnel (Li-bu Shang-shu),
also called the Minister of Heaven (Tian-guan).
The Minister of the Interior (Zǎizhǎi) and the Grand Chancellor (Tàizǎi);
the two Ministers of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū);
and the Ministry of Summer (Xiàguān).
He is also called the Grand Marshal (Dàsīmǎ).
Third is the Ministry of Population (Hùbù),
the Earth Official (Dìguān).
He is also called the Great Minister of Instruction (Dà Sītǒng).
The Ministry of Punishments (Xíngbù) is the Autumn Official, also called the Great Minister of Justice (Dà Sīkòu).
5. Ministry of Rites (Li-bu).
Official of the Spring Office;
also called the Chief of Evaluation (quan-chang). 6. Ministry of Works (Gong-bu).
The Winter Office (Dongguan),
also known as the Grand Minister of Works (Da Sikong).
Yu was the third minister to labor for twelve years in taming the floods.
He rode upon four types of vehicles: a carriage for traveling on land,
a boat for traveling on water,
and a sled for traveling through mud.
As the mountain journey proceeds, the carriage opens up the Nine Provinces: Jizhou lies to the east of the River; Hexi lies to the west of the River;
Hena lies to the south of the River;
and Hebei lies to the north of the River.
Yanzhou is situated to the southeast of the Ji River and extends to the He River to the northwest;
Qingzhou lies to the east and north of the sea.
To the southwest it reaches Mount Dai;
Xuzhou extends eastward to the sea and northward to Mount Dai.
To the south lies the Huai River.
Yangzhou is bounded to the north by the Huai River and to the south by the Huai River.
Mount Beishan in Jingzhou commands the region to the north and extends southward to Hengyang;
Mount Nanshan in Yuzhou commands the region to the southwest.
To the north it borders the River;
Liangzhou has Mount Hua to its east and the Black Water (Heishui) to its west.
Yongzhou is bounded on the west by the Black Water and occupies Longmen on the east;
the West River flows through nine channels.
He dammed nine marshes,
crossed over nine mountains,
and diverted nine rivers.
Yao bestowed upon him the dark jade tablet to announce his successful completion of the task;
Shun then recommended him to all under heaven as his successor. He occupied the throne for sixteen years, beginning in the year Jiashu and ending in Jiyou.
He traveled eastward on tour to Kuaiji, where he passed away.
His age was one hundred years.
His posthumous title was Shouchan.
The successful one was called Yu; he named the year *sui*.
He established the month of Yin as the first month of the year and composed the Da Xia music.
For burials, they used *jia* wood and burned earth to create [the coffin].
At that time, there was the clan of Fangfeng;
its members were forty feet tall.

Jiazi (8): Qi was the son of Yu; his mother transformed into stone—another account says he was born from within a stone. Guiwei: He ascended the throne and reigned for nine years—another account says ten. He performed the *jiao* and *di* sacrifices to his ancestors, offering the *di* sacrifice to the Yellow Emperor; Wenzu (the Ancestral Cultured) was honored at the suburban sacrifice, while Gun was paired with Heaven as the Ancestor. Zu (the Ancestor) was Zhuanxu, who was paired with Wenzu. Taizu (the Great Ancestor) was Yu, and Zong (the Honored Ancestor) was Qi. His father, Qi, established a temple and a *tiaotang*. There were five ancestral temples: Taizu Yu, two Zhao, and two Mu.
Jiazi (9): Taikang was the son of Qi.
While hunting in the Luo, he did not return for ten months.
His five sons composed songs to admonish him.
He subsequently lost his throne; Renchen (Ren-chen) was then established [as ruler].
He reigned for twenty-nine years.
Zhongkang, the younger brother of Taikang, ascended the throne in Xin-you.
Dìxiàng Zhòngkāng’s son moved the capital to Shānqīu;
he was killed by Hòuyì of Yǒuqióng, who usurped his throne.
Zhì reigned for twenty-eight years.
Hù succeeded him,
but after two years, he was killed by his minister Han Xuò.
Han Zuo killed Yi and established himself;
ten years later, he was slain by Xia’s minister Mi.
These three rulers together occupied the throne for a total of forty years.
Jiazi (the first day of the sexagenary cycle): Ten. Shao Kang was the son of Xiang.
His mother was of the Youreng clan.
He possessed one *cheng* of land.
There was a multitude of one *liu*;
they extinguished the *jiaoji* rebels and returned to the ancient domain of Yu.
This was the restoration.
He was enthroned on the day *guiwei*.
He reigned for forty-nine years. He built the *ji*, *tuo*, *mo*, *jiu*, and *ning* [altars]. Yao, the son of Shao Kang, was enthroned on the day *jiumao*.
Zhi reigned for seventeen years.
Gengshen, the son of Huaining, ascended the throne;
he held the position for twenty-six years.
The son of Manghuai, Bingxu, ascended the throne.
He ruled for eighteen years.
In the year Jiazi (the eleventh), Xie, the son of Mang, ascended the throne in the year Jiachen.
He reigned for sixteen years.
His son, Gengshen, the descendant of Budongxie,
ascended the throne and governed for fifty-nine years.
Huangting did not descend to his younger brother Jiji, who was not established on the throne.
He reigned for twenty-one years.
[The year] Jiazi was the twelfth. Jing, the son of Huangting, ascended the throne on the day Gengchen.
Zhizhang reigned for twenty years.
Kongjia did not produce a son;
he was devoted to serving ghosts and spirits.
He was licentious.
The virtue of the House of Xia declined, and the feudal lords rebelled against him; Xing Chou was subsequently established as ruler.
In the thirty-first year of his reign, King Tang was born.
Jiazi (the first day of the sexagenary cycle). [Gao] Kongjia’s son, Renshen, ascended the throne.
He ruled for eleven years.
Jie, the son of Fa-gao, ascended the throne in the year Gui-wei.
He reigned for ten years—some say eleven.
Jie was the son of Fa.
His name was Lü Gui.
He had a favorite lady from the Shi clan named Mo Xi, who was licentious,
addicted to wine, violent, cruel, and infatuated with sensual pleasures and alcohol.
With lofty palaces and carved walls, the people fell into a mire of suffering like charcoal;
he regarded remonstrance as sorcery,
executed Guan Longfeng, and burned the Yellow Charts.
Jiazi, the fourteenth day: the two ministers greatly abolished the Way of Xia.
At that time, there were two suns; brightness was obscured, and day and night separated from one another.

Tang attacked him and exiled him to the Southern Marsh, where he died; his posthumous title was "The Tyrant" (Jie), given because he violated benevolence and killed many. On the day Renyin, [Tang] ascended the throne and made An-yi his capital.
He ruled for fifty-two years.
In all, there were seventeen generations spanning a total of four hundred and thirty-two years. 18.

Yin (The House of Lei): Beginning with Tang the Completer, followed by Waibing, Zhongren, Taijia, Woding, Taigeng, Xiaojia, Yongji, Taemu, Zhongding, Wairen, Handanjia, Zuyi, Zuxin, Wojia, Zuding, Nangeng, Yangjia, Pangeng, Xiaoxin, Xiaoyi, Wuding, Zugeng, Zuajia, Linxin, Gengding, Wuyi, Taiding, and Dibo.
Di Xin. There were thirty rulers of the dynasty for a total of six hundred and twenty-nine years.
Jiazi (Gengzi), the fifteenth [generation]: surnamed Tang, zi Shi.
His ancestors were the descendants of Qi, the fourteenth-generation grandson of Ke, son of Gaosin.
His progenitor, [Shao] Hao, served as the Minister of Instruction under Yao and ruled during the Water Virtue (*shuǐdé*).

Dūmò (都亳) is the present-day Yǎnshī County; it is also called Yìshú (毅熟). Zhāomíng (昭明), Xiàngtǔ (相土), Chāngshēng (昌生), Cáowéi (曹圍), Míng (冥), Zhèn (振), Wēi (微), Bàodīng (報丁), Bàoyǐ (報乙), Bàobǐng (報丙), Zhǔrén (主壬), and Zhǔguǐ (主癸) begot Zǐlǚ (子履). His reign name was Lǚ, and his courtesy name was Tiānyǐ (天乙).
He was born on a Yi day.
He was the twenty-first descendant of the Yellow Emperor;
his ancestor was Qiè.
His mother was Jian Di;
she swallowed a dark egg,
and [the child] was born by being cleft from her back.
Qi was born from the son of Xuan-niao;
therefore, his clan name was Zi.
There were those who altered their blessings to include even birds and beasts. Xia Jie was unrighteous.
Take Yi Yin as an example when he served as prime minister:
he received the mandate to campaign against [the Shang];
when he campaigned to the east, the west felt resentment; when he campaigned to the south, the north felt resentment.
There was a great drought for seven years.
He reproached himself for six transgressions and burned his body;
only then did it rain.
It was established in the year Yiwei (the 13th year of Daizhi).
[The founder] lived to the age of one hundred; the month of Jianchu (the second lunar month) was established as the beginning of the year.

The years were designated as *si* (sacrifices), and the posthumous title was *Chuyu* (Eliminator of Tyranny and Remover of Cruelty). In later generations there was Pengzu, surnamed Jian and named Keng;
he was a worthy great officer.
He lived for eight hundred years,
was fond of recounting ancient events,
and was posthumously titled Pengzu.
Waibing, the second son of Tang, reigned for three years. Zhongren, the younger brother of Waibing, reigned for four years.
Taia was the eldest grandson of Tang and the son of Tading.
He remained in power but was not enlightened;
Yi Yin therefore banished him to Tonggong.
After three years, he repented his errors.
He was further welcomed back to Bo. He governed his position for thirty-three years. He established six ancestral shrines: two *zhao* (left) for Tāng and two *mu* (right) for Tàijiā.

At the suburban sacrifice (*jiǎosì*), he honored the First Ancestor (*zǔ*) Dìkù; Wénzǔ was the secondary ancestor (*zōng*). Míng was sacrificed at the suburban altar to be paired with Heaven; Qiè was the secondary ancestor. Tàijiā was the Father and was sacrificed as the Primary Ancestor (*tàizǔ*). *Zǔ* refers to Qiè; *zōng* refers to Tāng; and the Father is Tàijiā. Thus he performed the sacrifices.
Jiazi (16): Woding was installed by Taijia on the day Xin-si.
He reigned for thirty years; in his eighth year, Yi Yin died.
Taigeng, the younger brother of Woding, reigned for thirty years—though one source says twenty-five years.
The Record of Antiquity and the Present states that thirty-five years have passed.

Jiazi (the first year of the sexagenary cycle), the seventeenth [year]. Xiaojia and Taigeng ruled for seventeen years. In the second month of the seventh year, on the first day of the moon, Jia-shen, the calendar was commenced.
Yongji was the younger brother of Xiaojia; the governance of the Yin dynasty had fallen into decline for twelve years.
Jiazi [year], the eighteenth [of the reign]: Taiwu was the younger brother of Yongji.
When he first ascended the throne, he did not follow the Way.
The feudal lords rebelled against him.
He appointed Yi Yin’s son, Zhi, as prime minister, and the Way of Yin flourished once more; he governed for seventy-five years.
Zhongding, the son of Taibu, moved the capital from Bo to Kaifeng (Chenliu) and ruled for seventeen years—some say eleven. Jiazi was the nineteenth year.

Wairen, the younger brother of Zhongding, ruled for fifteen years. Hedanjia, the younger brother of Wairen, moved the capital back to Xiang; the Yin dynasty declined once more, and he ruled for nine years.
Zuyi (Zuoyi) and Danjia (Danzhi) further moved the capital to Geng,
which is present-day Pipi County in Hedong.
Wuxian held office and promoted good governance for nineteen years.
Jiazi (Year 1): The twentieth year; Zu Xin, son of Yi, reigned for sixteen years. ○ Wo Jia, younger brother of Zu Xin, reigned for twenty-five years.
○ Zu Ding, elder brother of Wo Jia and younger brother of Zu Xin, reigned for twenty-five years. ○ Nan Geng, son of Wo Jia, reigned for twenty-nine years.
Yangjia, the son of Zuding, reigned for seventeen years.
[The first day of the sexagenary cycle was] Jiazi. 21. Pangeng, the younger brother of Yangjia, changed the name of Yin to Shang.
He further moved the capital to Bo and ruled for eighteen years.
Xiao Xin, the younger brother of Pan Geng, ruled for twenty-one years;
the Way of Yin declined, and the people longed for the former emperors.
He composed the three chapters of the *Pan Geng*.
Jiazi (year 22). Xiao Yi’s younger brother [Xiao Xin] ruled for twenty-two years.
Wu Ding was the son of Xiao Yi.
Taking oral tradition as his guiding principle,
he cultivated virtue and disseminated good governance,
so that all under heaven rejoiced.
The Book of Documents says:
"During the three years of mourning for his father, Gaozong did not speak as the ruler.
The Rites say:
During the three-year mourning period, the ruler did not speak.
All officials listened as the Chief Minister governed for fifty-nine years.
His total lifespan was one hundred years.
Temple name: Gaozong. Jiazi (year).

Reigns 23 and 22 [of his predecessors]. Zugeng’s son, Wuding, ruled for seven years. Zujia, the younger brother of Zugeng, ruled for sixteen years; during his reign, the Way of Shang fell into decline.
Lingxin and Zu Jia reigned for six years. ○ Gengding was the younger brother of Lingxin;
he moved the capital to Chaoge, within the present-day borders of Weizhou, and reigned for twenty-one years.
Wu Yi was the son of Geng Ding.
He was unrighteous, treating the spirits with contempt and oppressing the people;
he went hunting in the regions between the Yellow River and the Wei River.
Wu Yi was struck dead by a violent thunderbolt in his fourth year.
*Jiazi* (24). Tai Ding, the son of Wu Yi, reigned for three years. ○ Di Yi, the son of Tai Ding; the Way of Shang declined during his reign of thirty-seven years.
Jiazi (the first day of the sexagenary cycle), 25: Zhou Xin.
Also named Shou, he was the son of Di Yi and the younger brother of Wei Zi Qi.
Qi’s mother was of low status;
thus, she could not succeed to the throne while he was at court.
Xin’s mother was the formal consort.
Chengzu did not speak of this;
internally he favored Daji,
and externally he employed E Lai.
He established pools of wine, groves of meat, and mounds of dregs;
he caused men and women to pursue one another therein in the nude,
and constructed palaces for eternal night.
One hundred and twenty days constitute one day and night.
They devised the "burning grid" (pao-lo) punishment and heated irons;
they clothed [the victims] in robes of precious jade and sliced open the hearts of worthy men.
He cut off the shins of those crossing the river at dawn.
When the feudal lords rose in rebellion,
King Wu conquered them.
He covered his head with his robes and threw himself into the fire to die.

In the thirty-first year of his reign, he was posthumously titled "Zan" (The Cruel); one who harms the good is called Zhou. Among the Yin, there were three men of humanity: Jizi, Weizi, and Shu Bi Gan. Dingwei then ascended the throne.
In total, there were thirty rulers who reigned for six hundred and twenty-nine years.

Zhou Lei said: "From the Zhou dynasty down to King Wen, King Wu, Kings Cheng, Kang, Zhao, Mu, Gong, Yi, Xiao, Yi, Li, Xuan, You, Zhu, Ping, Huan, Zhuang, Xi, Hui, Xiang, Jing, Kuang, Ding, Jian, Ling, Jing, Dao, Jing, Yuan, Zhen, Ai, Kao, Wei, Lie, An, Yi, Xian, Sheng, Shen, Jing, and Nan."
The thirty-first year of King Qin:
the seventh month, day seven;
the sixth year of the cycle, nineteen years [since the founding]: *jiǎzǐ*. Twenty-sixth year of King Wén, whose surname was Jī; he moved the capital to Hào during the reign of King Wǔ.
Now, the Prince of Jingzhao embodies the Wood Virtue.
His lineage originated with Houji; his mother, Empress Jangyuan, consort of Emperor Ku, conceived him after treading upon the footprint of a great man.
There were many such strange omens;
they were cast away in narrow alleys,
where even oxen and horses would not tread upon them.
He moved mountains to raise beasts and placed water there to nourish birds;
he then gathered them back in to rear them.
Therefore, his clan name was Qi.
He delighted in the work of planting;
Yao appointed him as the Minister of Agriculture (Biji).
His meritorious deeds were enfeoffed at Tai, where he was called Hou Ji.

His descendants included: Bu Zhu, Ju, Gong Liu, Qing Jie, Huang Pu, Cha Fu, Hui Yu, Gong Fei, Gao Yu, Ya Yu, Gong Zu Lei, and King Tai Wang Danfu—also known as Gu Gong—who fathered three sons: Taibo, Yuzhong, and Ji Li (the father of King Wen).
Originally, the state was based in Biin.
When Duke Gong moved to Qishan, his eldest and middle sons, knowing that Duke Gong intended to establish Ji Li as heir to pass the lineage to Chang,
fled to the Jing and Man tribes.
The establishment of the title "King" was intended to ensure the transmission of the lineage.
Regarding the records of the generations from ancient times to the present, there are differences between the *Shiji* (Records of the Grand Historian) and other sources.
According to these, the king's name was Chang, and he was the son of Ji Li.
One was named King Da Wang.
His younger son, Du Feng, became the Western Chief (Xibei) for Zhou.
Da possessed great virtue and wisdom; he occupied the throne for fifty years and lived to the age of ninety-seven.

The posthumous title *Wén* (Cultivated) is conferred upon those who are loyal and trustworthy and who receive guests with propriety. Based on the lines (*xiáo*) of the Eight Trigrams (*bāguà*), the *Zhōu Yī*: In the *Qián* hexagram, the first palace, the number is nine; thirty-six is the old Yang (*lǎo yáng*). In the *Kǎn* hexagram, the first palace, the number is seven; twenty-two is the young Yang (*shǎo yáng*). In the *Gèn* hexagram, the eighth palace, the number is seven; twenty-eight is the young Yang. In the *Zhèn* hexagram, the third palace, the number is seven; twenty-eight is the young Yang. In the *Xùn* hexagram, the fourth palace, the number is eight; thirty-two is the young Yin (*shǎo yīn*). In the *Lí* hexagram, the ninth palace, the number is eight; thirty-two is the young Yin. In the *Kūn* hexagram, the second palace, the number is six; twenty-four is the old Yin (*lǎo yīn*). In the *Duì* hexagram, the seventh palace, the number is eight; thirty-two is the young Yin.
Each hexagram contains six lines and the names of the six spirits,
which preside over matters of good and ill fortune.
These are known as the Azure Dragon (Qīnglóng), the Vermilion Bird (Zhūjué), the White Tiger (Báihù), the Dark Warrior (Wǔxú), the Flying Snake (Téngshé), and the Coiled Dragon (Gouchén).
Jiazi (the first year of the sexagenary cycle), the twenty-second week: Boyi and Shuqi were surnamed Mo.
They were men of virtue from Guzhu who heard that the Chief of Xi (King Wen) was skilled at nourishing the elderly, and they went to join him.
When the people of Yu and Rui had a dispute, they appealed to the Chief of Xi for arbitration.
Furthermore, he requested that Zhou be removed from the "burning pillar" execution.
Twenty: When King Wu issued his mandate and the Prince of Zhou, his elder brother, was established [as regent], he appointed Tai Gong Wang as his Grand Tutor.
Duke Dan of Zhou served as his chief counselor,
while the followers of Shao and Bi served as his attendants;
together they conspired to attack Zhou.
He raised an army at the Wei River.
Eight hundred feudal lords assembled there without prior appointment,
all of whom said:
"Zhou may be attacked.
On the day of Wumu, the troops reached Mengjin;
on the night of Guihai, they drew up their battle lines at the outskirts of Shang.
On the day of Jiǎzǐ, they fought at Mùyuè.
The soldiers in the vanguard turned their weapons against one another, and blood flowed so profusely that it floated the pestles of the mortars.
Having thus conquered Yīn.
Having brought great peace to the world, he retired his horses to the southern slope of Mount Hua and released his oxen beneath the Peach Grove; he laid down his weapons and spears.
He occupied the throne for seven years and lived to the age of ninety-three.
He was buried at Hao.
The posthumous title "Wu" (Martial) is given to one who overcomes and settles calamity and disorder; as the *Ritual* says:
"When there is a King over all under heaven..."
The ancient system for dividing land, establishing states, and founding capitals and towns was as follows:
the royal domain was one thousand *li* square;
a state of a Duke was one hundred *li* square.
A *hou* [duke] possessed seventy *li*;
a *bo*, *zi*, or *nan* [marquis, viscount, or baron] each possessed fifty *li*.
Those who did not reach this standard were called *fuyong* (dependent states).
The Zhou established the royal domain as one thousand li in extent;
a Duke’s territory was five hundred li,
and a Marquis’s four hundred li.
A Duke’s domain is three hundred li;
a Viscount’s is two hundred li;
and a Baron’s is one hundred li.
Regarding those who were not of sufficient rank, they were called *fuyong* (dependent states); they were buried with *sha* (funerary screens). The *Shiben* (Book of Origins) states:
"King Wu created the *sha*;
their shape was like that of a fan."
The walls were erected to decorate the coffins, which were set up on the day of Yi-mao.
Zi was established as the first month of the year.

The feudal lords of the fourteen states followed the King’s alternating enfeoffments, each producing their respective musical instruments: the Lei clan produced those for Zheng, Song, Jin, Wu, Wei, Qin, Qi, Lu, Chen, Si, Cao, Cai, Yan, Shao, Chu, and Man.
The feudal lords were fourteen.
Taibo of Wu, the son of King Tai,
fled with his younger brother Yuzhong to the Jingman tribes in the south.
He cut his hair and tattooed his body to show that he was unfit for use,
thereby avoiding King Ji-li;
thus the man of Jing was established as ruler.
His title was Gou.
During the reign of King Wu of Wu, he conquered Yin.
His posthumous title was Duke Wuchang.
Reaching the nineteenth generation from Shoumeng, they began to call themselves Kings;
Meng had four sons, the second of whom was named Jizha.
Da You was a man of great virtue and wished to establish Za as his successor; however,
Za yielded the position to his elder brother, Zhu Fan.
The people of Wu jointly established a sacrificial post (*zhā*).
Later, they abandoned it.
When they reached the sacrifice of Yu, they re-established the sacrificial post at Yanling.
From Taibo to Fuchai,
there were twenty-five generations;
then King Goujian of Yue extinguished them.
From Zhou Zhang to Fu Chai,
there were twenty-one rulers for a total of six hundred and fifty-five years.
This was during the time of King Jing. The *Liezi* states:
"Formerly, the Grand Chancellor of Wu asked Confucius, 'Master, are you a sage?
He replied, 'I, Qiu, am merely one of broad knowledge and strong memory.'"
They were not sages.
As for the Three Kings being called sages,
it was because the Three Kings made excellent use of wisdom and courage.
"Sageship is not something I know, O Qiu.
As for the Five Emperors who were sages,
it is said that the Five Emperors were skilled at employing benevolence and trustworthiness."
As for the sages, they are beyond what I, Qiu, can know.
Regarding the Three Sovereigns as sages,
it is said that the Three Sovereigns were adept at employing the administration of their times.
"As for the Sage, I do not know him.
Grand Chancellor Pi was startled and asked,
"If that is so, then who is the Sage?"
The Master paused for a moment, adjusted his expression, and replied:
"In the west there is a sage;
he does not govern, yet there is no disorder."
Without speaking, they inspire confidence;
without transforming, they act spontaneously.
Vast and boundless, the people are unable to give them a name.
Tai Gong Wang of Qi was also named Lü Shang.
He was a native of Donghai and his original surname was Jiang.
His ancestors had assisted Yu in the regulation of the waters and were enfeoffed at Lü.
King Wen received a divination sign of the "flying bear," and while hunting at the Wei River,
he met him there.
He said, "I have been looking for you for a long time.
Consequently, he was named Lü Wàng;
he was also known as Wǔshī.
He led the campaign against Zhou.
He was also named Shangfu.
He was enfeoffed at Yingqiu.
It is present-day Linzi in Qingzhou.
When Xiao Bai ascended the throne as Duke Huan,
he first became the hegemon.
From Taigong downward:

Dinggong (Lü Ji), Yigong, Jigong, Aigong, Hugong, Xiangong, Wugong, Ligong, Wenong, Chenggong, Zhuanggong, Līgong, Xianggong, Huanggong, Xiaogong, Zhaogong, Yigong, Huigong, Qinggong, Linggong, Zhuanggong, Jinggong, Ruzi, and Daogong; following Jianpinggong, Xuangong, and Kanggong, the state was usurped and extinguished by Tian He.
Together with the thirty rulers, they ruled for seven hundred and forty-seven years, corresponding to the seventeenth year of King An of the Zhou dynasty.
This was the period before and after Lord Jing, during which Guan Zhong, Bao Shu, Ning Qi, Yanzi, and their contemporaries lived.
Chen Hugong Man was a descendant of the Youyu clan.
His surname was Gui;
in ancient times, Shun was a commoner.
Yao gave him his two daughters in marriage, and he resided at Gui-na; consequently, this became his clan name.
When King Wu conquered Yin, he sought out the descendants of Shun.
He attained fullness [of his domain] and was enfeoffed in Chen to perform the sacrifices to Shun;
he was known as Duke Hu.
From Duke Hu downward,
there were twenty-three rulers: Shen, Huan, Xiao, Shen, You, Li, Wu, Ying, Ping, Wen, Huan, Li, Zhuang, Xuan, Mu, Gong, Ling, Cheng, Ai, Hui, Huai, and Min.
In the six hundred and fifty-third year,
the forty-first year of King Jing,
it was destroyed by Chu.
They sacrificed to Lord Donglou, a descendant of Xia Yu.
During the Yin dynasty, his lineage was sometimes enfeoffed and sometimes extinguished.
When King Wu conquered Yin, he established sacrifices for him in Chenliu.
This was the County of Yongqiu.
From Duke Donglou down to Duke Jian,
who reigned in the spring.
There were nineteen rulers for a total of five hundred and thirty-nine years;
in the twenty-fourth year of King Ding, the state was destroyed by the Lord of Chu, Duke Hui.
Cao Shuzhendo was the sixth son of King Wen and the younger brother of King Wu;
he was enfeoffed at Cao.
It is now Dingtao County in Jiyang.
When he reached Boyang,
he took pleasure in hunting and falconry.
He lost his state through negligence in governance.
Later, the Marquis of Cao turned his back on Jin and allied with Song.
This has been the case from the time of Zhenduo downwards.
Taibo, Zhongjun, Gongbo, Xiaobo, Yibo, King You, Daibo, Huibo, Guobo, King Mu, Kings Huan, Zhuang, Xi, Zhao, Gong, Wen, Xuan, Cheng, Wu, Ping, King Dao, Xiang, King Yin, King Jing, and Boyang.
The twenty-sixth generation;
six hundred and forty-five years;
the thirty-third year of King Jing.
It was for the sake of King Jing of Song that he destroyed it.
Cai Shudu was the fifth son of King Wen and the younger brother of King Wu.
After the conquest of Yin,
he enfeoffed Shu Xian at Guan and enfeoffed Du at Cai.
He appointed two officials to govern the remaining people of Yin:
Zhouzi Wugeng, also known as Lu Fu.
From Duke Zhu to Duke Qi,
there were twenty-seven rulers over a period of five hundred and twenty-seven years.
During the reign of King Ding,
it was destroyed by Chu.
Duke Zhou of Lu, Dan, was the fourth son of King Wen.
After King Wu conquered Yin,
he enfeoffed [the descendants of] Shao Hao at his ancient site,
which is present-day Xianyuan County in Yanzhou.
The Duke did not accept [the throne].
He remained to assist King Wu.
After King Wu passed away, he assisted King Cheng.
He sent his son, Boqin, to proceed to Lu in his stead.
The Duke admonished him, saying,
"I am the son of King Wen."
He was the younger brother of King Wu and the uncle of King Cheng;
even by the standards of the world, he was not of humble station.
Nevertheless, I wash my hair and grasp it three times;
I eat and spit out my food three times;
and I rise to wait upon scholars.
I fear you will lose the worthy men of the world.
Go to Lu, my son,
and do not use the state to pride yourself upon others.
Bo Qin received his mandate in Lu. From Bo Qin downward,
there were Kao, Yang, You, Wei, Li,
Xian, Zhen, Wu, Yi, Bo, Yu, Xiao, Hui, Yin, Huan, Zhuang, Min, Xi, Wen, Xuan, Cheng, Xiang, Zhao, Ding, Ai, Dao, Yuan, Mu, Gong, Kang, Jing, Ping, Wen, and Qing.
Thirty-four rulers for nine hundred and fifteen years;
it came to an end when King Kaolie of Chu destroyed it in the first year of the reign of Qin Zhuangxiang. From the beginning of the Spring and Autumn period under Duke Yin until the death of Duke Ai.
In the sixteenth year of Duke Ai, Confucius passed away.
Yan Shigong Xi was of the same surname as the Zhou;
when King Wu conquered Yin, he [was granted the territory].
He was enfeoffed in Yan.
During the time of King Cheng,
he was summoned to serve as one of the Three Ducal Ministers.
He governed Shaanxi,
winning the hearts of the myriad people.
He traveled on circuit through the various districts and towns.
There was a *gāntáng* tree;
he decided lawsuits beneath it.
When he summoned his soldiers and the people, they thought of him as their father.
Dare not cut down the trees;
thus they composed the "Poem on the Sweet Pear Tree.
This began from the time the Duke descended [from office].

Yuan Shiwang, Huï Hou, Lì Qīng, Āi Zheng, Miū Xuān, Huán Zhuāng, Xiāng Huán, Xuān Zhāo, Wǔ Wén, Yì Huì, Dào Yuán, Píng Jiǎn, Xiàn Xiào, Chéng Mǐn, Lì Huán, Wén Yì, Prince Zǐkuài, Zhāo Huì, Wǔ Chéng, Xiào Jīn, and Xǐ.
There were thirty-seven rulers for a total of eight hundred and ninety-four years,
until the First Emperor of Qin extinguished it.
21. King Cheng, named Song, was the son of King Wu; he resided in Luo and ascended the throne at the age of thirteen.
Duke Zhou acted as regent, establishing the rites and composing the music.
The world was harmonious and peaceful.
In the seventh year, he returned the administration to the King.
His dynasty was destined to last for thirty generations.
Its years were divined to last seven hundred;
it was governed for forty-seven years.
Duke Zhou established the rites and music of ruler and subject, and King Cheng praised him.

The Three Dukes were established: the Grand Preceptor (Taishi), the Grand Tutor (Taifu), and the Grand Guardian (Taobao). The Nine Ministers were as follows: first, the Minister of Ceremonies (Taichang) was in charge of music;
second, the Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial (Guanglu) was in charge of wine and food offerings;
third, the Minister of Justice (Dali) was in charge of penal law.
Fourth, the Lord of the Four Departments is the chief of the imperial relatives.
Fifth, the Lord of the Grand Treasury oversees the storehouses.
Sixth, the Minister of Agriculture oversees cultivation and planting.
Seventh, the Minister of Reception (Honglu) presides over foreign guests.
Eighth, the Grand Master of the Horse (Taipu) presides over chariots and horses.

He was a man of Xunyang in Nanjun. His ancestors had long resided in the region of Wu. His father, Sengxun, served as the Magistrate of Shanyin during the Qi dynasty. Sengchao was born with a noble countenance and a refined bearing. From childhood, he possessed a profound understanding of the Way and a deep affinity for the scriptures. At the age of seven, he entered the monastery of Huishou at Mount Lu to study under the Venerable Daohui. By the age of ten, he had mastered the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, and various other treatises. He also thoroughly investigated the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. His insight was sharp and his eloquence was swift; he was widely renowned throughout the land. At that time, the Venerable Daohui was lecturing on the *Dharmapada*; when he reached the passage concerning the "Three Vehicles," Sengchao suddenly rose from his seat and said, "The Buddha taught three vehicles to lead sentient beings to the path. However, the ultimate truth is that there is but one vehicle. Daohui was deeply impressed by this and remarked, "This boy is truly extraordinary. He then composed the *Dacheng xianshi lun* (Treatise on the Manifestation of Mahayana) in ten fascicles to explain the meaning of the One Vehicle. Sengchao read it and said, "This is merely a provisional teaching; it does not yet reach the ultimate principle. Daohui asked, "What is the ultimate principle? Sengchao replied, "The ultimate principle is that all dharmas are originally non-arising and non-ceasing; they are neither existent nor non-existent, and they transcend all verbal expression. Daohui sighed in admiration and said, "The Buddha has appeared in the world, and you have come to propagate his teachings. At that time, the Venerable Daohui was about to travel to the capital. Sengchao followed him to Jiankang. There, he encountered the Venerable Daorong, who was lecturing on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. When he reached the passage where Vimalakīrti asks Mañjuśrī, "From where do you come? Sengchao rose from his seat and said, "Mañjuśrī, you are traveling through the void; what 'coming' or 'going' can there be? Daorong was greatly pleased and said, "This youth is truly a vessel of the Dharma. He then composed the *Shi wuming lun* (Treatise on the Ten Non-existences) in ten fascicles to explain the meaning of the sutra. Sengchao read it and said, "This is still a provisional teaching; it does not yet reach the ultimate principle. Daorong asked, "What is the ultimate principle? Sengchao replied, "The ultimate principle is that all dharmas are originally non-arising and non-ceasing; they are neither existent nor non-existent, and they transcend all verbal expression. Daorong sighed in admiration and said, "The Buddha has appeared in the world, and you have come to propagate his teachings. Later, Sengchao traveled to the South Land and stayed at the monastery of Huishou at Mount Lu. He then went to the capital and resided at the monastery of Huiguan. During the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, he was summoned to the palace to lecture on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. The Emperor and his ministers were all deeply moved. He also lectured on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and the *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*. His disciples numbered over a thousand. In the third year of the Tianjia era, he fell ill and passed away at the age of sixty-two. He was buried at Mount Lu. His disciples erected a stupa at the foot of the mountain.

Emperor Yizong failed to fulfill his duties as a sovereign; his spirit was eclipsed by delusion.
He once again followed the tracks of those who had gone before him only to overturn them, wailing for grief upon a field of ignorance.
He offered up a portion of his own flesh as a sacrifice for the hundred-fold liberation [of sentient beings],
swearing an oath with his own life that he would have no further worldly attachments;
shedding tears, he prostrated himself in worship.
Although he served the ancestral temple and the Supreme Deity, there was nothing further he could advance;
he humbled himself despite the nobility of his ten-thousand-chariot state,
making himself equal to the ancient barbarians.
After several thousand years, he has distanced himself from them by sacrificing his own person as an offering.
Alas! His fortune is exhausted and his mandate is spent;
Heaven has announced this to him.
Emperor Yi passed away before three months had elapsed.
That the virtue of the Tang was not flourishing—
surely there were reasons for this!
The Commentary states:
How extreme was the severity with which Lord Song Jingwen reviled our former teacher!
I have repeatedly desired to rectify his words and offer him a rebuttal to dispel his satire.
Furthermore, having obtained Da Dian’s response to Zui’s discourse and Li Jie’s preface to his memorial,
everything that I intended to say has already been expressed by him.
Therefore, they are not discussed separately.
Furthermore, while the two emperors Xuanzong and Yizong were indeed excessively devoted [to Buddhism],
as for the High Ancestor (Gaozu), he purged the Three Teachings.
The imperial edict was issued and he was transferred from his post.
Emperor Wuzong extensively suppressed the followers of Śākyamuni;
before even a year had passed, he himself met with disaster.
This too must necessarily be feared.
Nevertheless, the True Buddha is the fundamental basis of both the sage and the ordinary person;
its essence is coextensive with the great void.
He employs his power in common with the multitudes;
he acts without striving and yet there is nothing he does not do;
he is nowhere and yet there is nowhere he is not.
Thus, those who perceive the Buddha as being external to the mind and worship him with excessive devotion do not possess right view; nor do those who,
being ignorant of the fundamental source, deliberately disparage him.
This is precisely to destroy oneself.
Jingwen censured the faults of his veneration while concealing the errors of his self-destruction.
How could this be called the work of a true historian?
10. Jiǎwǔ: Xīzōng Yǎn was the fifth son of [Emperor] Yì.
The eleventh [emperor] ascended the throne;
he passed away at the age of twenty-seven and was buried at Jingling.
The year of the *gān-fú* cycle: in this year, a commoner in Bingzhou gave birth to a child with two heads and four hands. On the day of Yimèi, the rebel Yu Xiánzhī gathered a multitude at Chángyuán.
Gāo Pián defeated the Nanzhào. Yu Xiánzhī incited a rebellion, and Huáng Cháo responded to him.
Jihai (10th day of the 11th month): On the first and second days of this month, two suns appeared together and fought.

Gengzi (17th day): The reign name was changed to Guangming. Tian Lingzi escorted the Son of Heaven westward. The rebel Chao entered Chang’an, established the state name as Dazhi, and adopted the era name Jintong. Li Kuyong fled to Dadan.
Xinchou (761): Zhonghe was changed [as the era name]; the Emperor himself entered Shu from Xingyuan. Toba Sigong led his troops to suppress the rebellion and was granted authority over Xia and Sui;
this marked the beginning of Western Xia as a military commandery. He served as the Regional Commander (Jiedushi).
11. Chan Master Shanhui of Jiaoshan in Lishu was a native of Xianting in Guangzhou.
His secular surname was Liao.
At the age of nine, he left home at Longya Mountain in Tanzhou and received full ordination according to his age.
He traveled to Jiangling to study the sutras and śāstras, thoroughly mastering the three trainings.
He subsequently entered a Chan assembly to apply himself with diligence to his practice and study.
Initially residing at Jingkou,
one night Daowu arrived there, leaning on his staff.
While attending the Master’s ascent to the hall,
a monk asked:
"What is the Dharma-body?"
The Master said,
"The Dharma-body is formless.
[The student] asked, "What is the Dharma-eye?"
The Master said,
"The Dharma-eye is without flaw.
The Master spoke again:
It cannot be grasped within the present moment.
Its intent lies within the present moment, yet it is not a dharma of the present moment; it is not something that can be reached by the ears or the eyes.
Daowu then laughed.
The Master then gave rise to a doubt, wondering why Daowu was laughing.
Daowu said:
"Master, you and those like you are peerless teachers in this world;
you should go to Huating County in Zhejiang to visit Master Boatman.
The Master said:
When asked whether he had found him, Daowu replied,
"That master has not a single tile to shelter his head above,
nor a spot of ground to set a锥 (a small awl) upon below."
The Master then changed his attire and went directly to Huating.
There he met Chuangzi (Fengxue), who was rowing his boat toward him.

Their spiritual affinity was so profound that not a single word was exchanged; seeing Chuangzi’s demeanor, Master Zizhang realized that the latter intended to withdraw from the world and forget all artifice.
Soon, scholars flocked together;
their dwellings were scattered like stars, and they gathered there for study day and night.
This was the year Gengyin of the tenth year of the Xiantong era of the Tang dynasty.
The assembly at Haizhong divined the site at Jia Shan, where the monastery was swiftly established.
The Master ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying:
"Since the time of the Patriarchs..."
People of that time misunderstood this and have passed it down to the present day,
taking the words of the Buddhas and patriarchs as models for human teachers.
In doing so, they instead become madmen who lack wisdom.
He merely pointed out to you that the non-existence of dharmas is itself the Way.
In the Way, there is not a single dharma, nor is there a Buddha to be realized.
There is no Way to be attained and no dharma to be abandoned.
Therefore it is said:
"There is no dharma before the eyes; the intent lies before the eyes.
This is not a dharma of the present moment.
If one studies toward the Buddhas and patriarchs,
this person has not yet attained the eye;
they remain entirely dependent upon the dharmas that serve as their support.
One cannot attain mastery.
Originally, because the realm of birth and death is vast and boundless, the nature of consciousness lacks any portion of freedom;
thus, one must travel thousands of miles and tens of thousands of leagues to seek out a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
One must possess the correct eye to forever escape erroneous views and definitively examine the birth and death before one's eyes:
do they truly exist,
or do they truly not exist?
If there is someone who definitely attains permission for the woman to emerge from her head,
those of superior capacity will clarify the Way upon hearing these words;
those of middling or inferior faculties will wander restlessly like waves.
"Why do you not decisively take hold [of liberation] within birth and death?
Where else could there be any doubt regarding the Buddha or the Patriarchs who would substitute themselves for your birth and death?
A person of wisdom would laugh at you."
The verse says:
Toiling under the laws of birth and death,
one seeks refuge only at the side of the Buddha.
Currently deluded regarding the correct principle,
one slaps at fire searching for a water bubble.
A monk asked:
"From the time of our predecessors, there has been the teaching of the Patriarchal Intent (zuyi) and the teaching of the Master’s Intent (jiaoyi).
Why do you, Venerable Sir, say here that these do not exist?
The Master replied:
For three years he did not eat rice,
yet there was no hungry person before his eyes.
[The Master] said, "Since there is no hungry person, [what is this hunger?]"
"Why does so-and-so not awaken?
The Master said,
"Precisely because awakening has caused you, O Kalyāṇamitra, to become deluded."
The Master spoke in verse: "Clearly luminous, there is no dharma of awakening;
the dharma of awakening, on the contrary, deludes people.
Stretch out both legs and sleep."
There is neither falsehood nor truth.
A monk asked:
"What is the realm of Jia Shan?"
The Master said:
"A monkey carries its young back into the green peaks;
a bird picks up a falling flower before the azure cliffs."
The Master reopened the profound pivot of the Dharma, and when nearly a decade had passed,
on the seventh day of the eleventh month of the first year of the Zhonghe era of the Tang dynasty (the Xinchou year),
he summoned his attendants and said:
I have discussed the Way with the assembly of monks for many years.
Each of you should know for yourselves the profound purport of the Buddha-dharma.
Now my illusory body reaches its end, and I shall depart.
"You daughters must protect yourselves well as you did when I was alive;
do not follow the common crowd by giving way to grief.
Having spoken these words, he passed away suddenly in the night.
On the twenty-ninth day of that month, he was interred at his home mountain.
He was seventy-seven years of age and fifty-seven years since his ordination.
An imperial edict conferred the posthumous title of Great Master Chuánmíng;
his stupa was named Yǒngjì.
On the eighth month of the Rényīn year, Zhu Wēn, who had been appointed as the Regional Defense Commissioner (Tiānfángyǎngshǐ) of Tóngzhōu by the Nest [of rebels], came to surrender.
He was granted the name Quan Zhong.
On the *gui-mao* day in the fourth month, Li Kuyong and others fought against Chao at Weiqiao and defeated him.
The Restoration of the Capital.
Jiachen (the 10th year of the Kaibao era), the seventh month: Li Shiyue pursued Huang Chao at Langhu Valley.
His nephew, Lin Yan, beheaded Chao and surrendered.
Yisi (the second year of Guangqi), the third month: the Emperor returned to the capital. In the twelfth month, the eunuch Tian Lingzi was defeated by Wang Chongrong; the Emperor fled to Fengxiang.
The troops of the Shatuo entered the capital,
plundering and setting it ablaze;
it was subsequently reduced to a wasteland of war.
From this point on, the world fell into fragmentation and great chaos.
(12) Dingwei: In this year, Chan Master Yantou Huo entered nirvana.
The Master was a native of Quanzhou.
His surname was Ke.
Having shaved his head in youth,
he traveled to Chang'an to receive full ordination.
He traveled to lecture halls to study the sūtras and vinaya.
Subsequently, he joined Xuefeng and Qinshan as companions to roam leisurely through the gardens of Chan.
He first visited Linji.
When Zhiyi was about to pass away, he saw Yangshan as soon as he entered the gate; holding up his sitting mat, he said, "Upādhyāya.

The Master said,

Shan said, "What are you doing?

The Master replied,

Xuefeng was serving as the head cook at Deshan’s monastery.
One day, because the meal was late,

Deshan then returned directly to his quarters.
Fengju brought this up for the Master to consider.
The Master said,

Upon hearing this, Mount Wenshu dispatched an attendant to summon the Master to the Abbot’s quarters.

The Master secretly revealed his intention.
On the following day, when Deshan ascended the hall,

Three years later, Deshan passed away.

The Master said,
"The sutra states:
'The intent of my teaching is like the three dots of the character for *yi*.'"
First, place a dot toward the east;
this opens the eyes of all bodhisattvas.
Second, place a dot toward the west.
Dotting [the syllable] with a single point activates the life-force of all bodhisattvas.
For the third [syllable], place one dot above and one below;
dotting [it] with a single point crowns the heads of all bodhisattvas.
This is the meaning of the first section.
It is further said:
"The intent of my teaching is like Maheśvara splitting open his face and thrusting out one eye."
This is the second section of meaning.
It further says:
"The intent of my teaching is like a drum smeared with lethal poison; it suffices for a single strike."
All who heard of it, whether far or near, were overcome with grief.
This is the meaning of the third section.
At that time, the Venerable Sōgan of Shōgan asked:
"What is the 'poison-coated drum'?
The Master pressed both hands upon his knees, leaned forward, and said,
"Han Xin at the imperial court."
Question: "In the midst of the vast expanse of dust, how does one discern the King?
The Master said:
"A copper gong filled to the brim with oil."
A question was asked: "What is the Way?
The Master said:
"Tear your straw sandals and throw them into the lake."
When someone asked about the Buddha, the Dharma, the Path, or Chan,
the Master would simply make a sound of sighing.
He once said to the assembly:
"When this old man departs, he will let out a great roar and go.
Subsequently, bandits rose up in the Central Plains,
and everyone fled their lands.
The Master sat upright and composed as before.
One day, a great number of bandits arrived and demanded that he provide them with provisions.
He then plunged his blade into him;
the Master’s countenance remained unmoved,
and he passed away with a great cry.
He lived to the age of sixty-one.
Later, during the Later Tang dynasty, he was posthumously honored with the title Great Master Qingyan (Pure and Austere).
He had a successor in the Dharma named Luoshan.
It is said that he was able to perpetuate his lofty style.
13. Wushen: The Wen-de era was changed.
In the third month, the Emperor passed away.
Jiyou (891): Emperor Zhaozong Huaiyi was the seventh son of Emperor Yizong.
He was exceptionally talented and possessed the ambition to restore the imperial house.
Externally, the threat had already materialized, while internally he lacked capable assistants;
thus, despite possessing wisdom and valor, he was unable to act.
At the age of thirty-eight, he was assassinated in his private chambers by Zhu Quanzhong and others.
He was buried at He-ling.
He reigned for sixteen years and changed the era name to Long-ji.

[This refers to] Maozhen of Xiqin.
Mao Zhen (reigned 37 years); Wu Xingmi (4 years); Yang Huainan (4 years);

His grandfather, Duo, and his father,

thereby causing the rulers of the Five Dynasties to feel such admiration and envy, is improper.

Indeed, among all worldly matters since antiquity, none is greater than birth and death. If one wishes to escape them, it lies in cultivating the six perfections and the myriad practices.
